architecture-audit.db16b243746de9f0d4f9455ec3562f41b4bd60b6:
schemaVersion: 1
name: architecture-audit
description: Architecture audit every 14 days — package and module dependency graph, cycles (including up-calls hidden in cross-module extensions of a shared type), layering drift against the repository's documented architecture, types spread across modules, public-surface width, concept placement, and split/merge candidates, measurement-first; reads one scored area in full and files up to 3 proposed improvement tasks plus measurement prerequisites
enabled: false
schedule:
  every_minutes: 20160
template:
  title: Architecture audit — file cycle, layering, abstraction, placement and split/merge tasks
  description: |-
    Audit this repository's architecture at package and module level: the
    dependency graph, cycles, layering, package splits and merges, and the
    abstractions that hold the layers together. File one proposed Orbit task
    per evidence-backed improvement. This task files work; it does not change
    code, and it never builds, tests, or times anything. The durable outputs
    are the filed tasks and the `architecture.json` artifact; the execution
    summary is the audit trail. A run that finds nothing above the bars below
    is a successful no-op when the scan evidence is persisted.

    Packages follow build and dependency boundaries, not taxonomy. A split,
    merge, or move needs dependency-graph evidence and a measured benefit,
    never conceptual tidiness alone.

    ## Rules and command surfaces

    - Use the registered Orbit tool surface, never direct lifecycle CLI
      subcommands (they skip agent provenance). Find the previous pass with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["done"],"type":"chore","tag":["architecture-audit","no-diff-expected"],"limit":1,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      and fetch its artifact with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.artifact.get --input '{"id":"<id>","path":"architecture.json","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Search coverage with
      `orbit tool run orbit.search --input '{"query":"<one distinctive token>","kind":"task","all":true,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      (lexical search matches one substring: use a single distinctive token,
      never a multi-word phrase, and never treat a 0-hit multi-word query as
      proof that nothing covers a finding). Inspect a candidate with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.show --input '{"id":"<id>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
    - Before filing, read the installed `orbit` skill's task-authoring
      reference and follow it for task shape. File an improvement (tool-created
      tasks start `proposed`) with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.add --input '{"title":"<title>","description":"<markdown>","acceptance_criteria":["<observable outcome>"],"context_files":["file:<verified path>"],"complexity":"<assessed>","tags":["arch-audit","tech-debt","<cycle|layering|package-split|package-merge|abstraction|placement>"],"type":"refactor","relations":[{"type":"spawned_from","target":"<this task ID>"}],"priority":"<low|medium>","workspace":"<current workspace path>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      File a measurement prerequisite with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.add --input '{"title":"Measure <candidate>: <what must be quantified>","description":"<markdown>","acceptance_criteria":["<observable outcome>"],"context_files":["file:<verified path>"],"complexity":"medium","tags":["arch-audit","tech-debt","no-diff-expected"],"type":"chore","relations":[{"type":"spawned_from","target":"<this task ID>"}],"priority":"<low|medium>","workspace":"<current workspace path>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      File a correctness defect confirmed in passing (see below) with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.add --input '{"title":"<title>","description":"<markdown with file:line evidence>","acceptance_criteria":["<observable outcome>"],"context_files":["file:<evidence source path>","file:<matching test path>"],"complexity":"medium","tags":["arch-audit"],"type":"bug","relations":[{"type":"spawned_from","target":"<this task ID>"}],"priority":"<low|medium|high|critical>","workspace":"<current workspace path>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Read each filed task back with `orbit.task.show` before recording it as
      delivered. Never file a finding without verified `context_files`. Chain
      dependencies between tasks filed in this run with a follow-up
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.update --input '{"id":"<filed task ID>","dependencies":["<predecessor task ID>"],"model":"<agent-family>"}'`,
      and read the task back to confirm the field took effect.
    - Static analysis only: no builds, tests, or timing runs in this task.
      Put throwaway scripts under `.orbit/tmp/` (`$ORBIT_SCRATCH_DIR`).
    - Fail open. A run that finds nothing above the bars is a successful
      no-op. Do not invent work to justify the run.

    ## What this sweep owns

    This sweep owns structure that only shows up repository-wide: edges
    between packages and top-level modules, cycles, where a concept lives,
    how large a package or shared type has grown, and whether the seams
    between layers are real. It does not own file size or module layout
    inside one package, dead code, duplication, local simplification, or one
    rule broken inside a single area — other sweeps and ordinary review own
    those. If you confirm a correctness defect in passing, file it as a `bug`
    tagged `arch-audit` with the payload above, per the task-authoring
    reference; it does not count toward the filing cap.

    ## Pin and cursor

    Fetch `__ORBIT_BASE_BRANCH__` and record the full SHA of its tip; read
    every file at that SHA. Read the previous pass's `architecture.json` (see
    above): it holds the previous metrics, the deferred candidates, and the
    area reviewed last time. Absent or unreadable means this is the baseline
    pass; say so.

    ## Discover the repository's shape

    Discover everything below from tracked files; hard-code nothing from
    another repository. Record each answer in the artifact:

    1. **Languages and packages.** From the tracked manifests and lockfiles,
       list each publishable or workspace-internal package (or module, in a
       single-package repository) and its source root. Exclude vendored and
       generated trees, build output, and test-only code from every count
       below, and name the exclusions.
    2. **The graph method.** Build the package and module dependency graph
       from the ecosystem's own metadata tool when the repository has one;
       otherwise fall back to a scan of import statements — and, inside the
       repository, of qualified paths and re-exports — over the discovered
       source roots. Name the method actually used, and its precision
       limits, in both the artifact and the execution summary.
    3. **The documented architecture**, when one exists: look for an
       architecture document at the repository root or under its docs tree
       (common names are an `ARCHITECTURE` file or `architecture` pages),
       design overviews, and the agent guides. Record which document, if
       any, states the intended layers or dependency direction.
    4. **The repository's own guards**: any tracked dependency-direction,
       layering, or lint check, and the CI configuration that runs it,
       discovered from the tracked CI and script files. A guard that exists
       but is not wired into CI is itself a lead, not evidence of direction.

    Examples — one per ecosystem; use only the row this repository matches
    and ignore the rest:
    - Rust example: metadata from `cargo metadata --format-version 1 --no-deps`, package manifests named `Cargo.toml`, source under each manifest's directory, and behavior attached to a type from another module in an inherent `impl` block.
    - Go example: metadata from `go list -json ./...`, modules declared in `go.mod`, and packages as directories of `.go` files.
    - JavaScript/TypeScript example: workspace packages from the root manifest's workspaces field or the package-manager workspace file, with import and re-export scanning inside each package.
    - Python example: distributions and packages from `pyproject.toml` or setup files, usually with an import scan as the graph source.
    - Cross-module extension examples: extension methods or partial classes, extension functions, protocol or type extensions, and reopened classes each attach behavior to a type from a module other than the one defining it.

    ## Pass A — structure metrics, whole repository, every run

    Scope is non-test sources under the discovered source roots. Record in
    the artifact, with deltas against the previous pass:

    1. **Package graph.** Every package with its non-test line count,
       dependency edges to other in-repository packages (production and
       test-only edges recorded separately), fan-in, and fan-out. When a
       documented architecture or a repository guard states an edge list or
       direction, diff the measured edges against it: an edge in code but
       not in the document, or the reverse, is a candidate.
    2. **Module graph and cycles.** Inside each package over 10,000 non-test
       lines, build a graph of the top-level source directories, and one
       level deeper for any directory over 20,000 lines. Draw an edge for
       each kind of reference:
       - every import of another in-repository module;
       - every fully qualified path or re-export pointing into another
         module;
       - **every call that resolves into behavior attached to a shared type
         from a module other than the caller's** (see the cross-module
         extension examples above).

       That last kind of edge matters. A shared type whose behavior is
       attached from several modules hides up-calls that an import-only map
       misses: a lower module can call a method whose implementation lives
       in an upper module, and no import line betrays it. Approximate these
       edges by indexing the member names each module attaches to each
       shared type, then searching other modules for calls to those names
       on that type. Record precision limits honestly.

       Report the strongly connected components (cycles) and each edge that
       violates a documented direction, with `file:line` examples.
    3. **Distributed types.** For each type whose behavior is attached from
       three or more top-level modules, or in more than 40 separate blocks
       or declarations in total, record the count per module. These types
       anchor the current package boundaries: they block splits, and they
       show where an interface owned by the lower layer, a port, or
       operations-as-data handlers would cut a seam.
    4. **Public surface.** Per package, count the exported items reachable
       from the package entry point, and how many no other in-repository
       package uses. An internal package whose public surface is much wider
       than its consumers use is a candidate.
    5. **Concept placement.** Types and functions with the same name stem
       defined in two or more packages (configuration, error, and record
       types, path helpers, identifier wrappers, subprocess or API
       wrappers). Read them before recording a candidate: a shared name is
       a lead, not a finding.
    6. **Size and rebuild reach.** Non-test lines per package, and per
       top-level directory of packages over 20,000 lines. Also count, for
       each package, the in-repository packages that would need to rebuild
       or re-check when it changes — its reverse-dependency closure.

    ## Layering: documented, or inferred

    When a documented architecture (Pass A discovery step 3) states the
    intended layers or dependency direction, judge edges against it, and use
    it for the layering-drift and placement lenses below.

    When no document states one, infer layers from the measured graph
    alone — for example by dependency depth: packages and modules that
    nothing in the repository depends on sit at the top, and those that
    depend on no other in-repository code sit at the bottom. Report the
    inferred layers, module by module, in the artifact and the execution
    summary. Inferred layers are a description of what exists, not an
    authority: without a documented architecture, file only true cycles
    (strongly connected components) and up-calls — an edge from a module
    into a module that already depends on it directly or transitively,
    including extension edges that close a cycle the import-only graph does
    not show — and file no layering-drift, placement, or abstraction tasks
    that rest on the inferred layering being right. Record such candidates
    in the artifact as deferred, with the reason "no documented
    architecture".

    ## Pass B — one area, read in full

    Pick one area for a full structural read: a package, or a top-level
    source directory of a package over 20,000 lines. Split it one level
    deeper while it exceeds 20,000 non-test lines. Score each area as
    `(cycle edges + violating edges + distributed-type blocks) × (1 + churn ÷ 1,000)`.
    Churn is the area's non-test lines changed since it was last reviewed,
    or over the last 30 days if it has never been reviewed. Skip an area
    when over half its files are in the `context_files` of an open
    `arch-audit` task, or of any in-progress or review task. Record every
    score.

    Read every non-test line of the module entry points, exported types, and
    interface definitions in the area, plus the files that hold its
    cross-module edges and distributed-type blocks. A search, sample, or
    truncated tool response is not a read. Judge the area's abstractions:
    what each layer owns, whether the seams are real (an interface or port
    with a clear owner, versus one shared type every layer extends), and
    where a concept is modelled twice.

    ## Lenses and bars

    Every finding must clear its bar; taste alone is never a finding.

    - **Cycle.** A module-level strongly connected component, or a single
      edge against a documented direction. Name the edge to cut and the
      mechanism: move the item to the lower layer, introduce an interface or
      port owned by the lower layer, invert with a callback, or move the
      caller up.
    - **Layering drift.** The documented architecture disagrees with the
      measured edges. The task decides which one changes and says why. This
      lens requires a documented architecture; without one, file nothing
      under it (see above).
    - **Package split.** A candidate whose dependency direction is already
      consistent, or becomes consistent once the named cycle tasks land,
      plus an expected measurable benefit estimated from rebuild reach and
      line share (Pass A item 6). This sweep never measures that benefit:
      file a **measurement task first** — a `no-diff-expected` chore that
      records the numbers the estimate rests on (full and incremental build
      or check timings on a stated host class, dependency and fan-in
      counts, or whichever quantity the benefit claim uses) and gives a
      go/no-go per candidate. Only then file the extraction task, with a
      `dependencies` entry on the measurement task, instructed to reject
      itself on a no-go. Name the distributed types from Pass A item 3 that
      anchor the boundary and how the extraction handles each one.
    - **Package merge or dissolve.** A package under about 1,500 non-test
      lines with a single in-repository consumer and no build, stability, or
      publishing reason to stand alone, or two packages that almost always
      change together (more than 70% co-change over 90 days of commit
      history). A merge is a restructuring like a split: file its
      measurement task first when the case rests on build or coupling
      numbers an estimate alone cannot settle.
    - **Move.** A module, type, or mechanism that belongs in a different
      existing package or layer under the documented architecture. A move
      whose case rests on unmeasured coupling or build claims also gets its
      measurement task first, never a direct restructuring task.
    - **Abstraction.** A concrete structural cost, stated in countable
      terms: a shared type that three or more layers extend, an interface
      with one implementer sitting in the wrong package, a public surface
      more than twice what its consumers use, or one concept modelled in
      two packages. Name the target shape and the steps to reach it.
    - **Placement.** A mechanism or contract that lives above the package
      the documented architecture says should own mechanisms or contracts
      of its kind, or that is defined independently in two or more packages
      with consumers in each. Name every copy and every consumer.

    ## Duplicate and conflict safety

    Before filing, list open work with
    `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["proposed","backlog","in-progress","review","blocked"],"tag":"arch-audit","limit":200,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
    Then search each finding's distinctive symbol with `orbit.search` (see
    above). Check rejected `arch-audit` tasks too, with
    `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["rejected"],"tag":"arch-audit","limit":200,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`:
    read the rejection rationale and refile only if the evidence has
    materially changed, saying what changed.

    - **Covered by an open task:** skip the finding, or add the new evidence
      to that task as a comment if it extends the task's scope.
    - **Touches a file in any in-progress or review task:** defer it to the
      next pass and record it in the artifact.
    - **Own chains:** chain the tasks filed in this run with
      `dependencies` (set by the follow-up `orbit.task.update` above): cycle
      cuts before the splits they enable, and measurement before
      extraction, merge, or move. Do not chain onto another sweep's
      proposed tasks.

    ## Filing

    File at most **3** improvement tasks per run, plus any measurement
    prerequisites they need; measurement prerequisites do not count toward
    the cap, and neither does an incidental `bug`. Rank candidates by
    structural value over risk: cycles first, then layering drift, then
    abstraction and placement, then splits, merges, and moves. Record the
    overflow in the artifact; the next pass files it first after
    re-verifying. File each improvement with the `orbit.task.add` payload
    above:

    - **Type and tags.** `type: refactor`; tags `arch-audit`, `tech-debt`,
      and the lens tag from the payload. A measurement prerequisite is a
      `chore` tagged `arch-audit`, `tech-debt`, and `no-diff-expected`.
    - **Complexity.** `hard` for anything that crosses a package boundary or
      moves an exported item; `xhard` for a package extraction or a change
      touching more than about 100 files. A measurement task is `medium`.
    - **`context_files`.** Verified `file:`/`dir:` selectors for every
      definition, edge, and call site that changes. For a split, merge, or
      move, also list the package manifests and lockfile, the documented
      architecture the filing cites (when one exists), the repository's
      dependency-direction guard (when it ships one), and, for a package
      that does not exist yet, its intended directory with
      `allow_missing_context: true`.
    - **Description.** It contains:
      - **Outcome**;
      - **Evidence**: the edges, cycle members, block counts, or metrics,
        with paths and line numbers at the pinned SHA, and the graph method
        that produced them;
      - **Target shape and steps**;
      - **Scope and non-goals**;
      - for a measurement task, the exact quantities to record, the commands
        that produce them (discovered from the repository's tracked build
        and CI configuration), the host class to run them on, and the
        go/no-go thresholds the restructuring decision uses;
      - the **Conventions** block below, copied verbatim.
    - **Acceptance criteria** for an improvement include:
      - The named edges, cycles, or placements are gone, and the
        repository's own dependency-direction or layering guard enforces
        the new direction wherever that guard can express it.
      - The documented architecture and any affected design overviews
        describe the result in the same change.
      - The exported names consumers use keep working, unless the task
        names the change.
      - The repository's own gate commands, discovered from its tracked
        files and agent guides, pass for the affected packages.
      - The execution summary lists every non-mechanical edit with its
        reason.
      - An extraction, merge, or move also reports the measured quantity
        its measurement task recorded, before and after, on the same host
        class.

    Conventions block:

    > - Behaviour-preserving. Public APIs, command and output shapes, and
    >   persisted data formats stay identical unless this task names the
    >   change.
    > - A new package edge updates the documented architecture and the
    >   repository's dependency-direction guard in the same change, when the
    >   repository has them.
    > - Keep moved code's visibility as narrow as before; do not widen an
    >   export, add a wildcard re-export, or silence an unused-import check
    >   to make a move compile.
    > - Prefer re-export shims for old paths over rewriting every import in
    >   one change, so concurrent work keeps merging; name the shim's
    >   retirement as a follow-up.
    > - An edge, caller, or consumer that this task does not list is a
    >   stop-and-report, not a judgement call.
    > - No layout-only moves; this task exists to change the dependency
    >   structure, not the file layout.

    Tasks land in `proposed`. Do not approve them.

    ## Handoff

    Write `.orbit/tmp/architecture.json` with:
    - `schema_version: 1`, `pinned_sha`, and `graph_method` — the metadata
      tool or import-scan method actually used, with its precision limits;
    - the documented architecture used, or the inferred layers when none
      exists;
    - the Pass A metrics (package graph, module edges, cycles, distributed
      types, public surface, placement leads, sizes, and rebuild reach),
      with deltas against the previous pass;
    - the area scores and the area reviewed (selectors, files read);
    - every finding (lens, evidence, and its disposition: filed ID,
      commented-onto ID, deferred with reason, or rejected with reason);
    - the overflow list.

    Attach it with
    `orbit tool run orbit.task.artifact.put --input '{"id":"<this task ID>","source_path":".orbit/tmp/architecture.json","path":"architecture.json","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
    The execution summary covers:
    - the graph method used (metadata tool or import scan) and its stated
      precision limits;
    - the package count and edge count against the previous pass;
    - the cycle count and largest cycle;
    - the top distributed types by module spread;
    - the area reviewed, its score, and the top five alternatives;
    - when no documented architecture exists, the inferred layers;
    - every finding mapped to its disposition.
  acceptance_criteria:
  - The pass is pinned to one `__ORBIT_BASE_BRANCH__` SHA recorded in `architecture.json`, and it reads the previous pass's `architecture.json` or states that it is the baseline pass.
  - The dependency graph comes from the ecosystem metadata tool this repository uses, or from an import scan when it has none, and the execution summary and `architecture.json` name the method and its precision limits.
  - Pass A records the package graph, the module graph including cross-module extension edges into shared types, strongly connected components, distributed types, public-surface counts, concept-placement leads, and sizes with rebuild reach, each with deltas against the previous pass, and no build, test, or timing command was run.
  - When a documented architecture exists, measured edges are diffed against it; when none exists, the execution summary and `architecture.json` report the inferred layers and only true cycles and up-calls are filed, with no layering-drift tasks.
  - The reviewed area was chosen by the recorded score formula, with conflicted areas skipped, and its entry points, exported types, interfaces, and cross-module edge files were read in full.
  - Every split, merge, or move candidate whose case rests on unmeasured numbers was filed first as a `no-diff-expected` measurement task with go/no-go thresholds, and its restructuring task carries a `dependencies` entry on that measurement task.
  - Open and rejected `arch-audit` tasks were checked before filing, findings touching in-progress or review tasks were deferred into `architecture.json`, and no duplicate task was filed.
  - At most 3 improvement tasks were filed, measurement prerequisites excluded, all `proposed` with a `spawned_from` relation to this task, verified `context_files`, the Conventions block, and the filing acceptance criteria above.
  - The run attaches `architecture.json` to this task and the execution summary maps every finding to a disposition; a run with no findings above the bars succeeds with that evidence and files no task.
  task_type: chore
  tags:
  - architecture-audit
  - no-diff-expected
  - tech-debt
  required_tools:
  - orbit.search
  - orbit.task.add
  - orbit.task.artifact.get
  - orbit.task.artifact.put
  - orbit.task.list
  - orbit.task.show
  - orbit.task.update
  priority: low
  complexity: hard
  status: backlog
dedupe: skip_if_open
created_by: system
created_at: 2026-10-24T00:00:00Z
updated_by: system
updated_at: 2026-10-24T00:00:00Z

backlog-hygiene.4c84ad7a63527d297d01ba42b3bf25b523f80074:
schemaVersion: 1
name: backlog-hygiene
description: Weekly report of stalled and untriaged tasks for human follow-up
enabled: false
schedule:
  cron: 30 7 * * 1
template:
  title: Report backlog hygiene candidates
  description: |-
    Produce one read-only backlog hygiene report for this workspace. The report
    is the task's persisted execution_summary; an empty report is a successful
    no-op. Snapshot the scan time in UTC and state the thresholds below.

    ## Safety and evidence

    - Do not change any task's status, approve, reject, dispatch, retry, resume,
      cancel, or mint work. Do not invoke status-changing task tools or workflow
      commands. Approval and disposition belong to a human. Do not edit Orbit
      state files directly. The only permitted write is this report through
      `orbit.task.update` with execution_summary; at most one comment per flagged
      task is optional and must contain no status change.
    - List each nonterminal status separately with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["blocked","in-progress","review","proposed","backlog","someday"],"limit":10000,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Check `truncated` and raise the limit if needed; a partial task corpus is
      not a clean scan. Inspect candidates and their dependencies with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.show --input '{"id":"<id>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Use the task's status-entry event in `history` to age blocked, in-progress,
      and review states; use `created_at` for proposed age. If history is absent,
      say which timestamp was substituted rather than implying certainty.
    - Read job runs through `orbit run history --limit <n> --json` and
      `orbit run show <run-id> --json`. Increase the history limit until it
      covers every candidate's linked `job_run_id` and the seven-day lookback;
      use the task's linked run as primary evidence. A missing run is unknown,
      not proof of failure. Do not read or edit the Orbit database.

    ## Candidate rules

    1. Blocked: status has lasted at least 7 days. Quote the latest blocking
       reason from task comments/history or description, and the linked run's
       state, completion time, and error when available. If either is absent,
       write "not recorded". Recommend the specific owner or credential check
       needed to unblock, without performing it.
    2. Orphaned: in-progress for at least 48 hours, or review for at least 7
       days, with no linked job run currently pending/running and no linked run
       started or finished in the last 48 hours. A missing linked run qualifies
       only after the status-age threshold. Check the linked run directly before
       labeling it orphaned; report its last known outcome or "no linked run".
       Recommend checking the worker or review owner before any re-dispatch.
    3. Proposed: created at least 14 days ago and still proposed. Group rows
       as likely duplicate, possibly already landed, or needs triage. Compare
       title/scope with open and closed tasks using
       `orbit tool run orbit.search --input '{"query":"<one distinctive term>","kind":"task","all":true,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
       and inspect plausible matches. Check `git log --all --oneline --grep=<task-id>`
       for each candidate. A log match is a lead, not proof that the exact work
       landed; inspect the commit before recommending closure. Never reject a
       task based on a title match alone.
    4. Dependency-unblocked but idle: backlog or someday tasks with at least
       one dependency, every dependency now done or rejected, and no status
       transition for at least 7 days after the last dependency entered its
       terminal status. Read each dependency's status and history; a rejected
       dependency may invalidate the task, so recommend reassessment rather
       than automatic pickup. If the latest terminal time is unavailable,
       report the uncertainty and do not claim the age threshold is met.

    ## Output

    Persist one execution_summary with scan time, thresholds, task and run
    coverage, and a Markdown table for each category. Every flagged row needs
    task id, age in the relevant status (or age since dependency clearance),
    concise evidence, and a recommended human action. Proposed rows also name
    their group and any duplicate task or candidate commit. A task may appear
    in more than one category; cross-reference rather than hiding it. Record
    counts and uncertainty explicitly. If no rows qualify, write the zero
    counts and "No action needed"; do not create filler work.
  acceptance_criteria:
  - The execution summary states scan time, thresholds, coverage, and a table for each of the four categories, with id, age, evidence, and recommended action for every flagged task.
  - Blocked rows include reason and linked run outcome; orphaned rows distinguish live, recent, missing, and terminal run evidence; proposed rows include duplicate and git-log checks; dependency rows verify every dependency's terminal status.
  - No task status was changed, no task was approved or rejected, and no work was dispatched; an empty scan is a successful no-op.
  task_type: chore
  tags:
  - backlog-hygiene
  - no-diff-expected
  required_tools:
  - orbit.task.list
  - orbit.task.show
  - orbit.search
  priority: medium
  complexity: medium
  crew: system
  status: backlog
dedupe: skip_if_open
created_by: system
created_at: 2026-09-24T00:00:00Z
updated_by: system
updated_at: 2026-09-24T00:00:00Z

schemaVersion: 1
name: backlog-hygiene
description: Weekly report of stalled and untriaged tasks for human follow-up
enabled: false
schedule:
  cron: 30 7 * * 1
template:
  title: Report backlog hygiene candidates
  description: |-
    Produce one read-only backlog hygiene report for this workspace. The report
    is the task's persisted execution_summary; an empty report is a successful
    no-op. Snapshot the scan time in UTC and state the thresholds below.

    ## Safety and evidence

    - Do not change any task's status, approve, reject, dispatch, retry, resume,
      cancel, or mint work. Do not invoke status-changing task tools or workflow
      commands. Approval and disposition belong to a human. Do not edit Orbit
      state files directly. The only permitted write is this report through
      `orbit.task.update` with execution_summary; at most one comment per flagged
      task is optional and must contain no status change.
    - List each nonterminal status separately with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["blocked","in-progress","review","proposed","backlog","someday"],"limit":10000,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Check `truncated` and raise the limit if needed; a partial task corpus is
      not a clean scan. Inspect candidates and their dependencies with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.show --input '{"id":"<id>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Use the task's status-entry event in `history` to age blocked, in-progress,
      and review states; use `created_at` for proposed age. If history is absent,
      say which timestamp was substituted rather than implying certainty.
    - Read job runs through `orbit run history --limit <n> --no-reconcile --json` and
      `orbit run show <run-id> --no-reconcile --json`. Increase the history limit until it
      covers every candidate's linked `job_run_id` and the seven-day lookback;
      use the task's linked run as primary evidence. A missing run is unknown,
      not proof of failure. Do not read or edit the Orbit database.

    ## Candidate rules

    1. Blocked: status has lasted at least 7 days. Quote the latest blocking
       reason from task comments/history or description, and the linked run's
       state, completion time, and error when available. If either is absent,
       write "not recorded". Recommend the specific owner or credential check
       needed to unblock, without performing it.
    2. Orphaned: in-progress for at least 48 hours, or review for at least 7
       days, with no linked job run currently pending/running and no linked run
       started or finished in the last 48 hours. A missing linked run qualifies
       only after the status-age threshold. Check the linked run directly before
       labeling it orphaned; report its last known outcome or "no linked run".
       Recommend checking the worker or review owner before any re-dispatch.
    3. Proposed: created at least 14 days ago and still proposed. Group rows
       as likely duplicate, possibly already landed, or needs triage. Compare
       title/scope with open and closed tasks using
       `orbit tool run orbit.search --input '{"query":"<one distinctive term>","kind":"task","all":true,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
       and inspect plausible matches. Check `git log --all --oneline --grep=<task-id>`
       for each candidate. A log match is a lead, not proof that the exact work
       landed; inspect the commit before recommending closure. Never reject a
       task based on a title match alone.

       one dependency, every dependency now done or rejected, and no status
       transition for at least 7 days after the last dependency entered its
       terminal status. Read each dependency's status and history; a rejected
       dependency may invalidate the task, so recommend reassessment rather
       than automatic pickup. If the latest terminal time is unavailable,
       report the uncertainty and do not claim the age threshold is met.

    ## Output

    Persist one execution_summary with scan time, thresholds, task and run
    coverage, and a Markdown table for each category. Every flagged row needs
    task id, age in the relevant status (or age since dependency clearance),
    concise evidence, and a recommended human action. Proposed rows also name
    their group and any duplicate task or candidate commit. A task may appear
    in more than one category; cross-reference rather than hiding it. Record
    counts and uncertainty explicitly. If no rows qualify, write the zero
    counts and "No action needed"; do not create filler work.
  acceptance_criteria:
  - The execution summary states scan time, thresholds, coverage, and a table for each of the four categories, with id, age, evidence, and recommended action for every flagged task.
  - Blocked rows include reason and linked run outcome; orphaned rows distinguish live, recent, missing, and terminal run evidence; proposed rows include duplicate and git-log checks; dependency rows verify every dependency's terminal status.
  - No task status was changed, no task was approved or rejected, and no work was dispatched; an empty scan is a successful no-op.

  tags:
  - backlog-hygiene
  - no-diff-expected
  required_tools:
  - orbit.task.list
  - orbit.task.show
  - orbit.search

  complexity: medium

blocked-task-triage.d195c06c2f382198a33427f4d5caa2dde97edd67:
schemaVersion: 1
name: blocked-task-triage
description: Hourly re-read of every escalated block, once per block episode; requeue mechanical blocks within the shared final-recovery requeue bound, propose scope amendments for decision blocks, and report human-only blocks
enabled: false
schedule:
  cron: 25 * * * *
template:
  title: Triage escalated blocked tasks
  description: |-
    Read every block episode awaiting triage in this workspace once, and record exactly one disposition for each through `orbit.task.block_triage`. The durable output is those task records; the execution summary is the audit trail.

    ## What qualifies

    Every block already got one recovery decision: final recovery in the pipeline, or the blocked-task backstop outside it. An episode (the task's latest move to `blocked`) awaits triage when that decision was an escalation, or when it has none and is older than the backstop's 72-hour limit. An episode already triaged, or touched by a human after the block (a comment, status change, artifact, or an unattributed field edit), is excluded. List them with `orbit tool run orbit.task.block_triage --input '{"action":"candidates","model":"<agent-family>"}'`. `qualifying` lists the episodes to triage; `excluded` lists the other blocked tasks and why. Zero qualifying episodes (the state changed since this task was minted) is a successful no-op.

    ## Rules

    - Record every decision with `orbit.task.block_triage`; it is the only write this run makes to a blocked task. It refuses an episode that no longer qualifies; report that refusal and move on.
    - Never complete, reject, archive or delete a task; never resume, retry or cancel a run; never edit any task's description, criteria, context, tags, crew or status through `orbit.task.update` (your own task's `execution_summary` excepted); never merge or close a pull request; never use `--force` or an operator-only tool (`orbit.task.requeue`, `orbit.workflow.run.resume`, `orbit.workflow.run.show`, `orbit.task.reject`, and the like). An operator-only route is a human action: report it.
    - Read evidence read-only: `orbit tool run orbit.task.show --input '{"id":"<task-id>","model":"<agent-family>"}'` (its `block` field names the cause, run and next action), `orbit run show <run-id> --no-reconcile --json`, the escalation comment the candidate list quotes, and `orbit tool run orbit.search --input '{"query":"<one distinctive token>","all":true,"model":"<agent-family>"}'` for related tasks and frictions. Quote the escalation reason exactly.

    ## Dispositions

    1. **Mechanical → requeue.** The cause is Orbit state or environment, and it has a documented, supported recovery this lane can apply: a crashed or interrupted run whose task can simply run again, stale state the next admission reconciles, or a transient provider or host failure that has since cleared (a later successful run on the same provider and host shows it). Apply any repair only through tools this lane holds, then call `orbit tool run orbit.task.block_triage --input '{"action":"requeue","id":"<task-id>","blocker":"<escalation reason, quoted>","reason":"<the repair applied and the evidence it cleared>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`. The tool counts the requeue against the final-recovery requeue bound (2 per 24 hours, one count shared with final recovery) and records `requeue n of 2 per 24h` on the task. Past the bound, for a task tagged `security` or `security-review`, or for a run another machine executed, it records a refusal naming the reason and leaves the task blocked: report that outcome. When it answers that the requeue count cannot be read, nothing was requeued: report the block as unresolved and do not retry another way. When the documented recovery needs an operator-only tool, a run resume or `--force` (explicit source repair of a stopped publication is one), report it with the exact operator command instead.
       When the cause is an Orbit defect with no supported recovery, file one friction record with `orbit tool run orbit.friction.add` (search for an existing one first), then report the block naming the friction. Never requeue it.
    2. **Decision → propose.** The block needs a scope or requirements choice: an out-of-scope behavior difference, an ambiguous or contradictory specification, or criteria that cannot be met as written. Call `orbit tool run orbit.task.block_triage --input '{"action":"propose","id":"<task-id>","blocker":"<escalation reason, quoted>","options":[{"summary":"<what the option decides>","consequences":"<what choosing it leads to>","replacement":"<the exact replacement text for each changed description section or criterion, ready to paste>"}, ...],"recommended":<1-based index>,"model":"<agent-family>"}'` with two or three options. The tool writes one comment and changes nothing else; the task stays blocked for the operator to choose.
    3. **Human-only → report.** Credentials or provider login; an owner sign-off the task names; a `security` or `security-review` tag; a block on a run executed on another machine whose evidence this owner cannot read (`job_run_machine` is not this host, `run_is_local` false); an OS or browser-kit requirement no reachable host meets. Call `orbit tool run orbit.task.block_triage --input '{"action":"report","id":"<task-id>","blocker":"<escalation reason, quoted>","reason":"<the specific human action>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`. Nothing else changes.

    When unsure between mechanical and another disposition, do not requeue: a block that recurs on one host must stay visible.

    ## Execution summary

    Persist an `execution_summary` listing every blocked task the candidate list read: task, block age, the escalation reason quoted, disposition, the action taken or proposed, and for requeues the bound count the tool returned (`requeue n of 2 per 24h`). List excluded tasks with the reason the candidate list gave. Record every refusal or tool error verbatim.
  acceptance_criteria:
  - Every qualifying block episode in the candidate list received exactly one `orbit.task.block_triage` decision (requeue, propose or report), or its refusal or error is recorded verbatim in the execution summary.
  - Every requeue went through `orbit.task.block_triage` and its comment records the shared bound count; no task was moved to backlog any other way, and a refused or unreadable count left the task blocked and reported.
  - Every decision proposal quotes the blocker and gives two or three options with consequences, ready-to-apply replacement text and a recommendation; no task's description, criteria, context, tags or status was edited.
  - Every human-only block names the specific human action, and an Orbit defect with no supported recovery has a friction record and was not requeued.
  - No task was completed, rejected or archived, no run was resumed, retried or cancelled, no pull request was merged or closed, and no operator-only tool or force path was used.
  - The execution summary lists every blocked task read with its age, quoted escalation reason, disposition, action and requeue count; zero qualifying episodes succeeds as a no-op.
  task_type: chore
  tags:
  - blocked-task-triage
  - no-diff-expected
  required_tools:
  - orbit.friction.add
  - orbit.search
  - orbit.task.block_triage
  - orbit.task.list
  - orbit.task.show
  priority: medium
  complexity: medium
  status: backlog
dedupe: skip_if_open
skip_unless_blocked_candidates: true

code-review.076c722f6ec06e51d4b1f9256851b82851e2bb6c:
schemaVersion: 1
name: code-review
description: Post-merge code review of changes merged since the last completed sweep
enabled: false
schedule:
  cron: 40 */6 * * *
template:
  title: Review recently merged changes
  description: |-
    Review the code merged into this workspace since the last completed sweep.
    The durable output is filed Orbit tasks for every confirmed finding plus the
    recorded review cursor; the execution summary is the audit trail. Narrative-only
    output does not count as delivery.

    ## Rules and command surfaces

    - Use the registered Orbit tool surface. Find the newest current-name sweep with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["done"],"type":"chore","tag":["code-review","no-diff-expected"],"limit":1,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      and the newest legacy-name sweep with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["done"],"type":"chore","tag":["code-review-sweep","no-diff-expected"],"limit":1,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Both tag filters use AND semantics. Compare the first result from each
      newest-first list by `created_at`, with the lexicographically smaller task ID
      winning an equal timestamp, and read the selected sweep's cursor with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.show --input '{"id":"<id>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      A finding is a `bug` tagged only `code-review`, so it is never a sweep
      candidate even when it completed after the selected sweep.
      Search existing coverage with
      `orbit tool run orbit.search --input '{"query":"<distinctive symptom, symbol, or file terms>","kind":"task","all":true,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      and list open review work with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["backlog","in-progress","proposed","blocked"],"tag":"code-review","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      File a finding with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.add --input '{"title":"<title>","description":"<markdown>","acceptance_criteria":["<observable outcome>"],"complexity":"medium","tags":["code-review"],"priority":"<low|medium|high|critical>","type":"bug","relations":[{"type":"regression_from","target":"<culprit task ID>"}],"workspace":"<current workspace path>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Omit `relations` only when no task in the window can be held responsible.
      Do not use direct lifecycle CLI subcommands; they skip agent provenance.
    - Fail open. A window with no confirmed findings is a successful no-op. Do not
      invent work to justify the run.

    ## Determine the review window

    Run both completed-sweep queries above and select the newer result using the
    stated ordering. Read the last-reviewed commit recorded in that sweep's
    execution summary, then review the commits from that point to the current HEAD
    of the workspace's integration branch. Never use a `code-review`-only finding
    as a cursor, and never treat a selected sweep's missing cursor as a first run.
    If neither sweep query returns a result, record the current HEAD as the baseline
    and stop — only that case seeds the cursor.

    ## Review the window

    Read the diffs white-box: correctness, concurrency and error handling, and
    conformance to the repository's documented standards (agent guide, contributing
    guide, lint configuration). Review the window as a whole — interactions between
    separately merged changes are findings per-change review cannot see.

    ## Attribute each finding to the task that introduced it

    Every finding is a regression from a change that landed in the window, so
    name the task that caused it. Find the commit that introduced the defect
    (`git log -L` or `git blame` on the offending lines, restricted to the
    reviewed range) and read the task ID from that commit: squash-merge subjects
    carry it as `[<task-id>]`, and the delivery's pull request references it
    otherwise. Confirm with `orbit.task.show` that the task exists and that its
    change is the one at fault — blame the commit that introduced the defect, not
    a later commit that merely touched the same file. When the defect spans
    several tasks' changes, blame the one whose change made the code wrong.
    When the culprit commit carries no task ID, or the defect predates the
    window and was only exposed by it, say so in the finding and file it without
    the relation rather than blaming a bystander.

    ## File confirmed findings

    Verify every finding against the live code before filing — a diff that looks
    wrong but is guarded elsewhere is not a finding. Search open Orbit tasks tagged
    `code-review` before filing; skip duplicates and nitpicks. File each confirmed
    finding as its own Orbit task with file:line evidence, a severity-appropriate
    priority, the `code-review` tag, and a `regression_from` relation targeting
    the task identified above. The finding's description names the culprit task
    and the commit that introduced the defect.

    ## Findings that narrow a shared invariant

    When a finding is a repair that narrows a shared invariant — what the host
    will create, what URLs are accepted, what counts as first-party, or any
    other predicate with more than one caller — search for every caller and
    fixture of that predicate and name them in the filed task's description;
    its acceptance criteria must require the same change to update all of
    them together, not just the call site that produced the observed symptom.

    A pull request that is green only against its own base is not evidence
    the merged tree is green. When the finding shares an invariant with other
    in-flight work, the filed task's acceptance criteria must require
    comparing the per-commit suite on the integration branch against its
    parent commit, not just a green check on the PR's own base.

    ## Record the cursor

    Always record the reviewed range and the new last-reviewed commit in the
    persisted execution summary — the next sweep's window starts there. Record
    the same commit as this task's machine-readable cursor artifact, which the
    scheduler reads to decide whether the next tick has anything to review:
    write `{"schema_version":1,"ref":"<integration branch>","cursor":"<full 40-character commit SHA>"}`
    to a gitignored scratch file inside the checkout (for example
    `target/sweep-cursor.json`) and attach it with
    `orbit tool run orbit.task.artifact.put --input '{"id":"<this task ID>","source_path":"target/sweep-cursor.json","path":"sweep-cursor.json","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
    Write it on every completed sweep, including an empty window: the commit it
    names is the one this sweep examined through, and a completed sweep without
    it leaves the next tick no cursor to compare the branch tip against.
  acceptance_criteria:
  - The review window was derived from the previous sweep's recorded cursor, or the current HEAD was seeded as the baseline on the first run.
  - Every filed finding was verified against live code, is non-duplicate, and carries file:line evidence with a severity-appropriate priority and the `code-review` tag.
  - Every filed finding carries a `regression_from` relation targeting the task whose landed commit introduced the defect, or its description states why no task in the window can be held responsible.
  - The reviewed range and the new last-reviewed commit are recorded in the persisted execution summary.
  - The new last-reviewed commit is attached as this task's `sweep-cursor.json` artifact (`schema_version` 1, the integration branch, and the full commit SHA).
  - A window with no confirmed findings succeeds as a no-op.
  task_type: chore
  tags:
  - code-review
  - no-diff-expected
  priority: medium
  complexity: hard
  # The portable system lane is seeded per machine and compatibility-aliased
  # for configs written before that crew existed.
  crew: system
  status: backlog
dedupe: skip_if_open
skip_if_unchanged:
  ref: __ORBIT_BASE_BRANCH__
  cursor:
    tags:
    - code-review
    - no-diff-expected
    legacy_tags:
    - code-review-sweep
    - no-diff-expected
created_by: system
created_at: 2026-08-23T00:00:00Z
updated_by: system
updated_at: 2026-08-23T00:00:00Z

schemaVersion: 1
name: code-review
description: Post-merge code review of changes merged since the last completed sweep
enabled: false
schedule:
  cron: 40 */6 * * *
template:
  title: Review recently merged changes
  description: |-
    Review the code merged into this workspace since the last completed sweep.
    The durable output is filed Orbit tasks for every confirmed finding plus the
    recorded review cursor; the execution summary is the audit trail. Narrative-only
    output does not count as delivery.

    ## Rules and command surfaces

    - Use the registered Orbit tool surface. Find the newest current-name sweep with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["done"],"type":"chore","tag":["code-review","no-diff-expected","auto-task:code-review"],"limit":1,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      and the newest legacy-name sweep with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["done"],"type":"chore","tag":["code-review-sweep","no-diff-expected"],"limit":1,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Both tag filters use AND semantics. Compare the first result from each
      newest-first list by `created_at`, with the lexicographically smaller task ID
      winning an equal timestamp, and read the selected sweep's cursor with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.show --input '{"id":"<id>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      A finding is a `bug` tagged only `code-review`, so it is never a sweep
      candidate even when it completed after the selected sweep. The
      `auto-task:code-review` provenance tag is carried only by tasks minted from
      this definition, so a hand-filed or full-review chore that shares the
      other tags never displaces a real sweep's cursor.
      Search existing coverage with
      `orbit tool run orbit.search --input '{"query":"<distinctive symptom, symbol, or file terms>","kind":"task","all":true,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      and list open review work with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["backlog","in-progress","proposed","blocked"],"tag":"code-review","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      File a finding with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.add --input '{"title":"<title>","description":"<markdown>","acceptance_criteria":["<observable outcome>"],"complexity":"medium","tags":["code-review"],"context_files":["file:<evidence source path>","file:<matching test path>"],"priority":"<low|medium|high|critical>","type":"bug","relations":[{"type":"spawned_from","target":"<this task ID>"},{"type":"regression_from","target":"<culprit task ID>","regression":{"nature":"<nature>","escape":"<escape>"}}],"workspace":"<current workspace path>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Omit the `regression_from` relation only when no task in the window can be
      held responsible. Derive canonical `file:` selectors from every evidenced
      source path, removing the line suffix, and add the matching
      regression-test location. Use existing paths where possible; for a test file
      that must be created, set `allow_missing_context: true` and identify that
      intended path. Never file a finding without context selectors.
      Do not use direct lifecycle CLI subcommands; they skip agent provenance.
    - Fail open. A window with no confirmed findings is a successful no-op. Do not
      invent work to justify the run.

    ## Determine the review window

    Run both completed-sweep queries above and select the newer result using the
    stated ordering. Read the last-reviewed commit recorded in that sweep's
    execution summary, then review the commits from that point to the current HEAD
    of the workspace's integration branch. Never use a `code-review`-only finding
    as a cursor, and never treat a selected sweep's missing cursor as a first run.
    If neither sweep query returns a result, record the current HEAD as the baseline
    and stop — only that case seeds the cursor.

    ## Review the window

    Read the diffs white-box: correctness, concurrency and error handling, and
    conformance to the repository's documented standards (agent guide, contributing
    guide, lint configuration). Review the window as a whole — interactions between
    separately merged changes are findings per-change review cannot see.

    ## Attribute each finding to the task that introduced it

    Every finding is a regression from a change that landed in the window, so
    name the task that caused it. Find the commit that introduced the defect
    (`git log -L` or `git blame` on the offending lines, restricted to the
    reviewed range) and read the task ID from that commit: squash-merge subjects
    carry it as `[<task-id>]`, and the delivery's pull request references it
    otherwise. Confirm with `orbit.task.show` that the task exists and that its
    change is the one at fault — blame the commit that introduced the defect, not
    a later commit that merely touched the same file. When the defect spans
    several tasks' changes, blame the one whose change made the code wrong.
    When the culprit commit carries no task ID, or the defect predates the
    window and was only exposed by it, say so in the finding and file it without
    the relation rather than blaming a bystander.

    ## File confirmed findings

    Verify every finding against the live code before filing — a diff that looks
    wrong but is guarded elsewhere is not a finding. Search open Orbit tasks tagged
    `code-review` before filing; skip duplicates and nitpicks. File each confirmed
    finding as its own Orbit task with file:line evidence, a severity-appropriate
    priority, the `code-review` tag, and a `regression_from` relation targeting
    the task identified above. The finding's description names the culprit task
    and the commit that introduced the defect.

    Classify every `regression_from` relation you file by adding
    `"regression":{"nature":"<nature>","escape":"<escape>"}` to it.
    Choose `unclassified` rather than guess. `nature` is what kind of regression
    the link records:
    - `broke_existing`: the culprit broke behavior that worked before it landed.
    - `defect_in_new`: the defect is in code the culprit itself introduced.
    - `incomplete`: the culprit shipped without part of what its task required.
    - `merge_reintroduced`: a merge restored code or assets an earlier change had removed.
    - `contract_drift`: docs, schemas or a contract drifted from the behavior the culprit shipped.
    - `unclassified`: the evidence does not settle the nature.
    `escape` is why the delivery gates missed it:
    - `no_test`: no test covered the broken behavior.
    - `test_not_selected`: a covering test existed but the delivery's gates did not run it.
    - `platform_only`: it shows only on a platform or host the gates did not exercise.
    - `review_missed`: it was visible in the diff and review did not flag it.
    - `spec_ambiguous`: the task or spec left the expected behavior open to the shipped reading.
    - `nondeterministic`: it depends on timing, ordering or environment and passed when gated.
    - `unclassified`: the evidence does not settle the escape.

    ## Findings that narrow a shared invariant

    When a finding is a repair that narrows a shared invariant — what the host
    will create, what URLs are accepted, what counts as first-party, or any
    other predicate with more than one caller — search for every caller and
    fixture of that predicate and name them in the filed task's description;
    its acceptance criteria must require the same change to update all of
    them together, not just the call site that produced the observed symptom.

    the merged tree is green. When the finding shares an invariant with other
    in-flight work, the filed task's acceptance criteria must require
    comparing the per-commit suite on the integration branch against its
    parent commit, not just a green check on the PR's own base.

    ## Record the cursor

    Always record the reviewed range and the new last-reviewed commit in the
    persisted execution summary — the next sweep's window starts there. Record
    the same commit as this task's machine-readable cursor artifact, which the
    scheduler reads to decide whether the next tick has anything to review:
    write `{"schema_version":1,"ref":"<integration branch>","cursor":"<full 40-character commit SHA>"}`
    to a gitignored scratch file inside the checkout (for example
    `.orbit/tmp/sweep-cursor.json`) and attach it with
    `orbit tool run orbit.task.artifact.put --input '{"id":"<this task ID>","source_path":".orbit/tmp/sweep-cursor.json","path":"sweep-cursor.json","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
    `orbit tool show <tool.name>` prints the tool's schema.
    Write it on every completed sweep, including an empty window: the commit it
    names is the one this sweep examined through, and a completed sweep without
    it leaves the next tick no cursor to compare the branch tip against.
  acceptance_criteria:
  - The review window was derived from the previous sweep's recorded cursor, or the current HEAD was seeded as the baseline on the first run.

  - Every filed finding carries a `regression_from` relation targeting the task whose landed commit introduced the defect, classified with a `regression` nature and escape (`unclassified` when the evidence does not settle one), or its description states why no task in the window can be held responsible.
  - The reviewed range and the new last-reviewed commit are recorded in the persisted execution summary.
  - The new last-reviewed commit is attached as this task's `sweep-cursor.json` artifact (`schema_version` 1, the integration branch, and the full commit SHA).
  - A window with no confirmed findings succeeds as a no-op.
  task_type: chore
  tags:
  - code-review
  - no-diff-expected
  required_tools:
  - orbit.search
  - orbit.task.add
  - orbit.task.list
  - orbit.task.show
  priority: medium
  complexity: hard
  status: backlog

    tags:

    - no-diff-expected
    - auto-task:code-review

      candidate even when it completed after the selected sweep. The
      `auto-task:code-review` provenance tag is carried only by tasks minted from
      this definition, so a hand-filed or full-review chore that shares the
      other tags never displaces a real sweep's cursor.
      Search existing coverage with
      `orbit tool run orbit.search --input '{"query":"<distinctive symptom, symbol, or file terms>","kind":"task","all":true,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      and list open review work with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["backlog","in-progress","proposed","blocked"],"tag":"code-review","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      File a finding with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.add --input '{"title":"<title>","description":"<markdown>","acceptance_criteria":["<observable outcome>"],"complexity":"medium","tags":["code-review"],"priority":"<low|medium|high|critical>","type":"bug","relations":[{"type":"spawned_from","target":"<this task ID>"},{"type":"regression_from","target":"<culprit task ID>"}],"workspace":"<current workspace path>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.

      held responsible.
      Do not use direct lifecycle CLI subcommands; they skip agent provenance.

      invent work to justify the run.

    ## Determine the review window

    Run both completed-sweep queries above and select the newer result using the
    stated ordering. Read the last-reviewed commit recorded in that sweep's
    execution summary, then review the commits from that point to the current HEAD
    of the workspace's integration branch. Never use a `code-review`-only finding
    as a cursor, and never treat a selected sweep's missing cursor as a first run.
    If neither sweep query returns a result, record the current HEAD as the baseline
    and stop — only that case seeds the cursor.

    ## Review the window

    Read the diffs white-box: correctness, concurrency and error handling, and
    conformance to the repository's documented standards (agent guide, contributing
    guide, lint configuration). Review the window as a whole — interactions between
    separately merged changes are findings per-change review cannot see.

    ## Attribute each finding to the task that introduced it

    Every finding is a regression from a change that landed in the window, so
    name the task that caused it. Find the commit that introduced the defect
    (`git log -L` or `git blame` on the offending lines, restricted to the
    reviewed range) and read the task ID from that commit: squash-merge subjects
    carry it as `[<task-id>]`, and the delivery's pull request references it
    otherwise. Confirm with `orbit.task.show` that the task exists and that its
    change is the one at fault — blame the commit that introduced the defect, not
    a later commit that merely touched the same file. When the defect spans
    several tasks' changes, blame the one whose change made the code wrong.

    window and was only exposed by it, say so in the finding and file it without
    the relation rather than blaming a bystander.

    Verify every finding against the live code before filing — a diff that looks
    wrong but is guarded elsewhere is not a finding. Search open Orbit tasks tagged
    `code-review` before filing; skip duplicates and nitpicks. File each confirmed
    finding as its own Orbit task with file:line evidence, a severity-appropriate
    priority, the `code-review` tag, and a `regression_from` relation targeting
    the task identified above. The finding's description names the culprit task
    and the commit that introduced the defect.

    ## Findings that narrow a shared invariant

    When a finding is a repair that narrows a shared invariant — what the host
    will create, what URLs are accepted, what counts as first-party, or any
    other predicate with more than one caller — search for every caller and
    fixture of that predicate and name them in the filed task's description;
    its acceptance criteria must require the same change to update all of
    them together, not just the call site that produced the observed symptom.

    the merged tree is green. When the finding shares an invariant with other
    in-flight work, the filed task's acceptance criteria must require
    comparing the per-commit suite on the integration branch against its
    parent commit, not just a green check on the PR's own base.

    ## Record the cursor

    Always record the reviewed range and the new last-reviewed commit in the
    persisted execution summary — the next sweep's window starts there. Record
    the same commit as this task's machine-readable cursor artifact, which the
    scheduler reads to decide whether the next tick has anything to review:
    write `{"schema_version":1,"ref":"<integration branch>","cursor":"<full 40-character commit SHA>"}`
    to a gitignored scratch file inside the checkout (for example
    `.orbit/tmp/sweep-cursor.json`) and attach it with
    `orbit tool run orbit.task.artifact.put --input '{"id":"<this task ID>","source_path":".orbit/tmp/sweep-cursor.json","path":"sweep-cursor.json","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
    `orbit tool show <tool.name>` prints the tool's schema.
    Write it on every completed sweep, including an empty window: the commit it
    names is the one this sweep examined through, and a completed sweep without
    it leaves the next tick no cursor to compare the branch tip against.
  acceptance_criteria:
  - The review window was derived from the previous sweep's recorded cursor, or the current HEAD was seeded as the baseline on the first run.
  - Every filed finding was verified against live code, is non-duplicate, and carries file:line evidence with a severity-appropriate priority and the `code-review` tag.
  - Every filed finding carries a `regression_from` relation targeting the task whose landed commit introduced the defect, or its description states why no task in the window can be held responsible.
  - The reviewed range and the new last-reviewed commit are recorded in the persisted execution summary.
  - The new last-reviewed commit is attached as this task's `sweep-cursor.json` artifact (`schema_version` 1, the integration branch, and the full commit SHA).
  - A window with no confirmed findings succeeds as a no-op.
  task_type: chore
  tags:
  - code-review
  - no-diff-expected
  required_tools:
  - orbit.search
  - orbit.task.add
  - orbit.task.list
  - orbit.task.show
  priority: medium
  complexity: hard

  # for configs written before that crew existed.
  crew: system
