schemaVersion: 1
name: code-review
description: Steady whole-tree code review that reviews the two least recently reviewed modules in full
enabled: false
schedule:
  cron: 40 */6 * * *
template:
  title: Review the two least recently reviewed modules
  description: |-
    Review this workspace's whole tree a little at a time: partition the tracked
    tree into modules, pick the two modules reviewed least recently, and read
    both in full at one pinned commit. The durable output is filed Orbit tasks
    for every confirmed finding plus the recorded rotation and cursor records;
    the execution summary is the audit trail. Narrative-only output does not
    count as delivery. This is not a review of a merged-commit window: a
    whole-module read also finds defects older than any recent change, and
    per-delivery diff review is a separate concern owned elsewhere.

    ## Rules and command surfaces

    - Use the registered Orbit tool surface. List prior rotation sweeps, newest
      first, with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["done"],"type":"chore","tag":["code-review","no-diff-expected","auto-task:code-review"],"limit":50,"fields":["id","created_at"],"model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      If the envelope reports `truncated`, repeat with a larger `limit` until it
      does not, so no completed sweep is left out of the rotation history.
      Both tag filters use AND semantics. The `auto-task:code-review`
      provenance tag is carried only by tasks minted from this definition, so a
      hand-filed or full-review chore that shares the other tags is never a
      rotation sweep, and a finding is a `bug` tagged only `code-review`, so it
      is never a sweep either.
      For each listed sweep, discover its artifacts before fetching any record:
      list them with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.show --input '{"id":"<id>","field":"artifacts","model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      and fetch the rotation record with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.artifact.get --input '{"id":"<id>","path":"reviewed-modules.json","model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      only when that listing names `reviewed-modules.json`.
      Search existing coverage with
      `orbit tool run orbit.search --input '{"query":"<distinctive symptom, symbol, or file terms>","kind":"task","all":true,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      and list open review work with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["backlog","in-progress","proposed","blocked"],"tag":"code-review","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      File a confirmed high or critical finding as its own task with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.add --input '{"title":"<title>","description":"<markdown>","acceptance_criteria":["<observable outcome>"],"complexity":"medium","tags":["code-review"],"context_files":["file:<evidence source path>","file:<matching test path>"],"priority":"<low|medium|high|critical>","type":"bug","relations":[{"type":"spawned_from","target":"<this task ID>"},{"type":"regression_from","target":"<culprit task ID>","regression":{"nature":"<nature>","escape":"<escape>"}}],"workspace":"<current workspace path>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      File a module's grouped medium and low findings as its single cleanup task with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.add --input '{"title":"<title>","description":"<markdown listing every grouped finding>","acceptance_criteria":["<observable outcome>"],"complexity":"medium","tags":["code-review"],"context_files":["file:<evidence source path>","file:<matching test path>"],"priority":"<low|medium>","type":"bug","relations":[{"type":"spawned_from","target":"<this task ID>"},{"type":"regression_from","target":"<culprit task ID>","regression":{"nature":"<nature>","escape":"<escape>"}}],"workspace":"<current workspace path>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      In the grouped payload, `context_files` is the deduplicated union of every
      grouped finding's selectors, and `relations` carries at most one
      classified `regression_from` entry per distinct culprit task among the
      attributable grouped findings (omit it for a finding no task can be held
      responsible for, and say why in the description; keep every grouped
      finding listed in the description, including findings that share a
      culprit; when grouped findings sharing a culprit have conflicting nature
      or escape classifications, state the differing classifications in the
      description and classify the single `regression_from` link
      `unclassified`). In either payload, omit
      the `regression_from` relation only when no landed task can be held
      responsible. Derive canonical `file:` selectors from every evidenced
      source path, removing the line suffix, and add the matching
      regression-test location. Use existing paths where possible; for a test file
      that must be created, set `allow_missing_context: true` and identify that
      intended path. Never file a finding without context selectors.
      Do not use direct lifecycle CLI subcommands; they skip agent provenance.
    - Fail open. A run whose two modules hold no confirmed findings is a
      successful no-op. Do not invent work to justify the run.

    ## Pin the commit

    Fetch the workspace's integration branch and record the full 40-character
    SHA of its tip. Partition, selection counts and every read use the tree as
    it stands at that SHA (`git show <sha>:<path>` when the checkout has
    moved), so later merges cannot shift a module under the review.

    ## Partition the tree into modules

    The module bound is **25,000 tracked text lines**, a maximum, not a target
    that may be exceeded. This is the same partition rule the whole-tree
    snapshot review uses, with no language- or toolchain-specific rule, so both
    definitions agree on what a module is. Inventory tracked files with
    `git ls-tree -r -z <sha>` and count each text blob at that SHA
    (`git show <sha>:<path>`), including an unterminated final line. Do not
    measure the moving checkout or count a concatenated archive containing
    binary files. Include source, tests, documentation and authored assets,
    including files at the root. Vendored, generated, binary and
    lockfile-only content may be excluded; record every excluded path and its
    reason in the execution summary and in `reviewed-modules.json`.

    Start with directory boundaries: take directories as candidates first.
    Recursively split every candidate above 25,000 lines into disjoint child
    directories, keeping files directly in the parent as separate candidates.
    If a leaf directory is still too large, split it into disjoint file sets.
    Prefer module boundaries where they fit the bound; the bound takes
    precedence. Group small, closely related candidates only when their
    combined count stays within the bound. Every included file must belong to
    exactly one module. Use `dir:` selectors for whole directories and `file:`
    selectors for direct files or file sets; never select an entire parent
    alongside its children in different modules. A module's ID is its
    selectors: the module's selectors sorted lexicographically and joined with
    `,`. Before selecting, verify all module counts against the bound and
    reconcile the inventories for gaps and duplicates. If a single included
    file exceeds 25,000 lines and this rule cannot produce a bounded module
    covering it, report `review_incomplete` with that uncovered path and
    count; do not file an oversized module review, silently exclude the file,
    or record it as reviewed.

    ## Build the last-reviewed map and select two modules

    The last-reviewed map comes only from `reviewed-modules.json` artifacts on
    done chores carrying `auto-task:code-review`, read as above — never from
    execution-summary prose, `sweep-cursor.json`, or a finding. Work through
    the listed sweeps newest first (newer `created_at` first, the
    lexicographically smaller task ID winning an equal timestamp): the first
    record that names a module ID is that module's most recent review, giving
    its review time (that sweep's `created_at`) and its pinned SHA. A sweep
    whose artifact listing has no `reviewed-modules.json`, or whose record is
    unreadable, malformed or names another schema version, counts as
    reviewing nothing — legacy window sweeps reviewed nothing in this
    rotation. Ignore modules the current partition no longer contains.

    A module that grew past the bound since its last review is split by the
    partition above, and each child inherits the last-reviewed time and pinned
    SHA of the module it was split from: when a current module has no record
    under its own ID, expand each recorded module's selectors to the file set
    they covered at that record's pinned SHA, and a current module whose
    files are a subset of one recorded module's files inherits that record.
    When more than one recorded module covers a current module's files, it
    inherits the oldest of their last-reviewed times and that record's pinned
    SHA.

    Count the commits since the last review for every module: for a reviewed
    or inheriting module, the number of commits in
    `<last reviewed pinned SHA>..<pinned SHA>` that touch the module's paths
    (`git rev-list --count <from>..<pinned SHA> -- <module paths>`); for a
    never-reviewed module, every commit up to the pinned SHA that touches its
    paths. Order all current modules by: never-reviewed first; then oldest
    last-reviewed time; then more commits since the last review; then the
    smaller module ID. Select the first **2** (every module when the partition
    holds fewer than 2). Record the ordering evidence — each selected
    module's last-reviewed time and pinned SHA or never-reviewed state, its
    commit count, and its ID — in the execution summary.

    ## Review the two selected modules in full

    Read each selected module in full at the pinned SHA, not a diff. On the
    first read, divide its inventory into stable named read partitions of at
    most 10,000 lines each. Prefer directory and module boundaries; split
    files larger than a partition into explicit inclusive line ranges. Cover
    every included line exactly once, with no gaps or overlaps, and include
    empty files in the inventory. Read every partition in full. Use parallel
    read passes or subagents when the crew and execution rules support them;
    otherwise read partitions sequentially. The reviewer remains responsible
    for reconciling every partition and checking calls and invariants across
    their boundaries. A search, summary, sampled read or truncated tool
    response does not count as a full read; continue in chunks until all
    lines in the partition have been examined.

    Look for:
    - correctness: logic errors, wrong edge cases, broken invariants between
      callers and callees;
    - error handling: swallowed or mislabelled errors, panics reachable from
      input, partial writes left behind on failure;
    - concurrency: races, lock ordering, locks held across awaits, unbounded
      or leaked tasks;
    - security boundaries: path traversal, injection, trust of unvalidated
      input, secrets in logs or output;
    - resource bounds: unbounded buffers, queues, retries, recursion or file
      growth;
    - conformance to the repository's documented standards: its agent guide,
      contributing guide, standards documents and lint configuration;
    - tests that do not test what they claim: assertions that cannot fail,
      fixtures that bypass the code under test, names that promise behavior
      the body never exercises.

    If full reading of a selected module cannot be met, do not record that
    module as reviewed and do not claim a clean no-op for it: return
    `result.blocker` with `kind: review_incomplete` and evidence naming each
    uncovered partition, file or unread line range and unresolved check, and
    put the same inventory in the execution summary. Only a module with every
    partition fully read and checks across partitions resolved counts as
    reviewed in this run.

    ## Attribute each finding to the task that introduced it

    Name the task that caused each finding when a landed task can be held
    responsible. Find the commit that introduced the defect (`git log -L` or
    `git blame` on the offending lines at the pinned SHA) and read the task ID
    from that commit: squash-merge subjects carry it as `[<task-id>]`, and
    the delivery's pull request references it otherwise. Confirm with
    `orbit.task.show` that the task exists and that its change is the one at
    fault — blame the commit that introduced the defect, not a later commit
    that merely touched the same file. When the defect spans several tasks'
    changes, blame the one whose change made the code wrong. When the culprit
    commit carries no task ID, or the defect predates every task that can be
    held responsible and was only exposed later, say so in the finding and
    file it without the relation rather than blaming a bystander. A
    whole-module review reaches defects far older than any recent change;
    age alone never makes a bystander responsible.

    ## File confirmed findings

    Verify every finding against the code at the pinned SHA before filing — a
    line that looks wrong but is guarded elsewhere is not a finding. Search
    open Orbit tasks tagged `code-review` before filing; skip duplicates and
    nitpicks. Give each confirmed finding a severity — `critical`, `high`,
    `medium` or `low` — used as the filed task's priority, file:line evidence
    at the pinned SHA, the `code-review` tag, and its module's ID.

    File each confirmed `critical` or `high` finding as its own `bug` task.
    Group a module's `medium` and `low` findings into at most one cleanup
    `bug` per module: it lists each grouped finding with its title, severity,
    file:line evidence and culprit task or the reason none can be held
    responsible; its `context_files` are the deduplicated union of the
    grouped findings' selectors; its priority is the highest grouped severity
    (`medium` when any grouped finding is medium, otherwise `low`); and it
    carries at most one classified `regression_from` relation per distinct
    culprit task among the attributable grouped findings (when findings sharing
    a culprit differ in nature or escape, note both in the description and
    classify the single link `unclassified`). A module with no medium or low findings files no cleanup
    task. Never group a high or critical finding into a cleanup task, and
    never file more than one cleanup task for one module in one run.

    Classify every `regression_from` relation you file by adding
    `"regression":{"nature":"<nature>","escape":"<escape>"}` to it.
    Choose `unclassified` rather than guess. `nature` is what kind of regression
    the link records:
    - `broke_existing`: the culprit broke behavior that worked before it landed.
    - `defect_in_new`: the defect is in code the culprit itself introduced.
    - `incomplete`: the culprit shipped without part of what its task required.
    - `merge_reintroduced`: a merge restored code or assets an earlier change had removed.
    - `contract_drift`: docs, schemas or a contract drifted from the behavior the culprit shipped.
    - `unclassified`: the evidence does not settle the nature.
    `escape` is why the delivery gates missed it. Inspect the tests and gate
    selection at the culprit commit: use `no_test` when no test exercises the
    broken behavior there, and `test_not_selected` when a covering test exists
    but the culprit's gates did not run it. Use `unclassified` only when the
    evidence does not settle the escape, and state the unresolved evidence in
    the finding's description. Mere visibility in the diff is not evidence
    for `review_missed` when no test exercises the broken behavior.
    - `no_test`: no test exercised the broken behavior at the culprit commit.
    - `test_not_selected`: a covering test existed at the culprit commit but its gates did not run it.
    - `platform_only`: it shows only on a platform or host the gates did not exercise.
    - `review_missed`: it was visible in the diff and review did not flag it.
    - `spec_ambiguous`: the task or spec left the expected behavior open to the shipped reading.
    - `nondeterministic`: it depends on timing, ordering or environment and passed when gated.
    - `unclassified`: the evidence does not settle the escape; state why in the finding.

    ## Findings that narrow a shared invariant

    When a finding is a repair that narrows a shared invariant — what the host
    will create, what URLs are accepted, what counts as first-party, or any
    other predicate with more than one caller — search for every caller and
    fixture of that predicate and name them in the filed task's description;
    its acceptance criteria must require the same change to update all of
    them together, not just the call site that produced the observed symptom.

    A pull request that is green only against its own base is not evidence
    the merged tree is green. When the finding shares an invariant with other
    in-flight work, the filed task's acceptance criteria must require
    comparing the per-commit suite on the integration branch against its
    parent commit, not just a green check on the PR's own base.

    ## Record the rotation and the cursor

    On every completed run, write the rotation record to
    `.orbit/tmp/reviewed-modules.json` and attach it with
    `orbit tool run orbit.task.artifact.put --input '{"id":"<this task ID>","source_path":".orbit/tmp/reviewed-modules.json","path":"reviewed-modules.json","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
    Its shape is
    `{"schema_version":1,"ref":"<integration branch>","pinned_sha":"<full 40-character commit SHA>","modules":[{"id":"<module ID>","selectors":["<selector>"],"line_count":123,"filed_finding_ids":["<filed task ID>"]}],"exclusions":[{"path":"<path>","reason":"<reason>"}]}`.
    List exactly the modules this run fully reviewed (both selected modules,
    or every module when fewer than 2 exist), each with its ID, its selectors,
    its measured line count and the IDs of every task filed for its findings
    — each individual high or critical task, and the module's cleanup task
    once when one was filed. A module this run did not fully read is never
    listed. The next run's last-reviewed map is built only from these
    records, so a completed run without one leaves its modules
    never-reviewed.

    Always record the same pinned commit as this task's machine-readable
    cursor artifact, which the scheduler reads to decide whether the next
    tick has anything to review: write
    `{"schema_version":1,"ref":"<integration branch>","cursor":"<full 40-character commit SHA>"}`
    to a gitignored scratch file inside the checkout (for example
    `.orbit/tmp/sweep-cursor.json`) and attach it with
    `orbit tool run orbit.task.artifact.put --input '{"id":"<this task ID>","source_path":".orbit/tmp/sweep-cursor.json","path":"sweep-cursor.json","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
    `orbit tool show <tool.name>` prints the tool's schema.
    Write it on every completed run, including a run with no confirmed
    findings: the commit it names is the pinned SHA this run examined, and a
    completed run without it leaves the next tick no cursor to compare the
    branch tip against.

    Record in the execution summary the integration branch and pinned SHA,
    the partition (every module's ID, selectors and line count, with every
    exclusion and its reason), the selection ordering evidence for the two
    reviewed modules, per-partition reading coverage for each, and every
    filed task ID (naming the cleanup task's module and grouped findings, and
    each individual task's finding). State explicitly when a reviewed module
    held no confirmed findings.
  acceptance_criteria:
  - The tracked tree was partitioned at one pinned integration-branch SHA into disjoint modules of at most 25,000 tracked text lines each, directory boundaries first, with every exclusion named, and the 2 modules selected were the least recently reviewed (never-reviewed first, then oldest last-reviewed time, then more commits since the last review, then the smaller module ID), or every module when fewer than 2 exist.
  - Each selected module was read in full at the pinned SHA in read partitions of at most 10,000 lines covering every included line exactly once, and incomplete reading is reported as `review_incomplete` with its uncovered partitions, files or ranges, never as a clean no-op.
  - The last-reviewed map was built only from `reviewed-modules.json` artifacts on done chores carrying `auto-task:code-review`; a sweep without a readable artifact counted as reviewing nothing, and a split module's children inherited its last-reviewed time.
  - Every filed finding was verified against the pinned SHA, is non-duplicate, and carries file:line evidence with a severity-appropriate priority and the `code-review` tag; each critical or high finding is its own `bug`, and each module's medium and low findings are grouped into at most one cleanup `bug` for that module listing every grouped finding, unioning their `context_files`, and carrying at most one classified `regression_from` per distinct culprit of an attributable grouped finding.
  - Every attributable filed finding carries a `regression_from` relation targeting the task whose landed commit introduced the defect, classified with a `regression` nature and escape (`unclassified` when the evidence does not settle one), or its description states why no landed task can be held responsible.
  - The reviewed modules are attached as this task's `reviewed-modules.json` artifact (`schema_version` 1, the pinned SHA, and per module its ID, selectors, line count and filed finding IDs) and the pinned SHA is attached as this task's `sweep-cursor.json` artifact (`schema_version` 1, the integration branch, and the full commit SHA), on every completed run including one with no confirmed findings.
  - A run whose reviewed modules hold no confirmed findings succeeds as a no-op.
  task_type: chore
  tags:
  - code-review
  - no-diff-expected
  required_tools:
  - orbit.search
  - orbit.task.add
  - orbit.task.artifact.get
  - orbit.task.artifact.put
  - orbit.task.list
  - orbit.task.show
  priority: medium
  complexity: hard
  status: backlog
dedupe: skip_if_open

  ref: __ORBIT_BASE_BRANCH__
  cursor:
    tags:
    - code-review
    - no-diff-expected
    - auto-task:code-review
    legacy_tags:
    - code-review-sweep
    - no-diff-expected

code-review.721a3f8b89b870bef2a258b88225f59c1ce90733:
schemaVersion: 1
name: code-review
description: Post-merge code review of changes merged since the last completed sweep
enabled: false
schedule:
  cron: 40 */6 * * *
template:
  title: Review recently merged changes
  description: |-
    Review the code merged into this workspace since the last completed sweep.
    The durable output is filed Orbit tasks for every confirmed finding plus the
    recorded review cursor; the execution summary is the audit trail. Narrative-only
    output does not count as delivery.

    ## Rules and command surfaces

    - Use the registered Orbit tool surface. Find the newest current-name sweep with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["done"],"type":"chore","tag":["code-review","no-diff-expected","auto-task:code-review"],"limit":1,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      and the newest legacy-name sweep with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["done"],"type":"chore","tag":["code-review-sweep","no-diff-expected"],"limit":1,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Both tag filters use AND semantics. Compare the first result from each
      newest-first list by `created_at`, with the lexicographically smaller task ID
      winning an equal timestamp, and read the selected sweep's cursor with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.show --input '{"id":"<id>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      A finding is a `bug` tagged only `code-review`, so it is never a sweep
      candidate even when it completed after the selected sweep. The
      `auto-task:code-review` provenance tag is carried only by tasks minted from
      this definition, so a hand-filed or full-review chore that shares the
      other tags never displaces a real sweep's cursor.
      Search existing coverage with
      `orbit tool run orbit.search --input '{"query":"<distinctive symptom, symbol, or file terms>","kind":"task","all":true,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      and list open review work with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["backlog","in-progress","proposed","blocked"],"tag":"code-review","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      File a finding with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.add --input '{"title":"<title>","description":"<markdown>","acceptance_criteria":["<observable outcome>"],"complexity":"medium","tags":["code-review"],"context_files":["file:<evidence source path>","file:<matching test path>"],"priority":"<low|medium|high|critical>","type":"bug","relations":[{"type":"spawned_from","target":"<this task ID>"},{"type":"regression_from","target":"<culprit task ID>"}],"workspace":"<current workspace path>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Omit the `regression_from` relation only when no task in the window can be
      held responsible. Derive canonical `file:` selectors from every evidenced
      source path, removing the line suffix, and add the matching
      regression-test location. Use existing paths where possible; for a test file
      that must be created, set `allow_missing_context: true` and identify that
      intended path. Never file a finding without context selectors.
      Do not use direct lifecycle CLI subcommands; they skip agent provenance.
    - Fail open. A window with no confirmed findings is a successful no-op. Do not
      invent work to justify the run.

    ## Determine the review window

    Run both completed-sweep queries above and select the newer result using the
    stated ordering. Read the last-reviewed commit recorded in that sweep's
    execution summary, then review the commits from that point to the current HEAD
    of the workspace's integration branch. Never use a `code-review`-only finding
    as a cursor, and never treat a selected sweep's missing cursor as a first run.
    If neither sweep query returns a result, record the current HEAD as the baseline
    and stop — only that case seeds the cursor.

    ## Review the window

    Read the diffs white-box: correctness, concurrency and error handling, and
    conformance to the repository's documented standards (agent guide, contributing
    guide, lint configuration). Review the window as a whole — interactions between
    separately merged changes are findings per-change review cannot see.

    ## Attribute each finding to the task that introduced it

    Every finding is a regression from a change that landed in the window, so
    name the task that caused it. Find the commit that introduced the defect
    (`git log -L` or `git blame` on the offending lines, restricted to the
    reviewed range) and read the task ID from that commit: squash-merge subjects
    carry it as `[<task-id>]`, and the delivery's pull request references it
    otherwise. Confirm with `orbit.task.show` that the task exists and that its
    change is the one at fault — blame the commit that introduced the defect, not
    a later commit that merely touched the same file. When the defect spans
    several tasks' changes, blame the one whose change made the code wrong.
    When the culprit commit carries no task ID, or the defect predates the
    window and was only exposed by it, say so in the finding and file it without
    the relation rather than blaming a bystander.

    ## File confirmed findings

    Verify every finding against the live code before filing — a diff that looks
    wrong but is guarded elsewhere is not a finding. Search open Orbit tasks tagged
    `code-review` before filing; skip duplicates and nitpicks. File each confirmed
    finding as its own Orbit task with file:line evidence, a severity-appropriate
    priority, the `code-review` tag, and a `regression_from` relation targeting
    the task identified above. The finding's description names the culprit task
    and the commit that introduced the defect.

    ## Findings that narrow a shared invariant

    When a finding is a repair that narrows a shared invariant — what the host
    will create, what URLs are accepted, what counts as first-party, or any
    other predicate with more than one caller — search for every caller and
    fixture of that predicate and name them in the filed task's description;
    its acceptance criteria must require the same change to update all of
    them together, not just the call site that produced the observed symptom.

    A pull request that is green only against its own base is not evidence
    the merged tree is green. When the finding shares an invariant with other
    in-flight work, the filed task's acceptance criteria must require
    comparing the per-commit suite on the integration branch against its
    parent commit, not just a green check on the PR's own base.

    ## Record the cursor

    Always record the reviewed range and the new last-reviewed commit in the
    persisted execution summary — the next sweep's window starts there. Record
    the same commit as this task's machine-readable cursor artifact, which the
    scheduler reads to decide whether the next tick has anything to review:
    write `{"schema_version":1,"ref":"<integration branch>","cursor":"<full 40-character commit SHA>"}`
    to a gitignored scratch file inside the checkout (for example
    `.orbit/tmp/sweep-cursor.json`) and attach it with
    `orbit tool run orbit.task.artifact.put --input '{"id":"<this task ID>","source_path":".orbit/tmp/sweep-cursor.json","path":"sweep-cursor.json","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
    `orbit tool show <tool.name>` prints the tool's schema.
    Write it on every completed sweep, including an empty window: the commit it
    names is the one this sweep examined through, and a completed sweep without
    it leaves the next tick no cursor to compare the branch tip against.
  acceptance_criteria:
  - The review window was derived from the previous sweep's recorded cursor, or the current HEAD was seeded as the baseline on the first run.
  - Every filed finding was verified against live code, is non-duplicate, and carries file:line evidence with a severity-appropriate priority and the `code-review` tag.
  - Every filed finding carries a `regression_from` relation targeting the task whose landed commit introduced the defect, or its description states why no task in the window can be held responsible.
  - The reviewed range and the new last-reviewed commit are recorded in the persisted execution summary.
  - The new last-reviewed commit is attached as this task's `sweep-cursor.json` artifact (`schema_version` 1, the integration branch, and the full commit SHA).
  - A window with no confirmed findings succeeds as a no-op.
  task_type: chore
  tags:
  - code-review
  - no-diff-expected
  required_tools:
  - orbit.search
  - orbit.task.add
  - orbit.task.list
  - orbit.task.show
  priority: medium
  complexity: hard
  # The portable system lane is seeded per machine and compatibility-aliased
  # for configs written before that crew existed.
  crew: system
  status: backlog
dedupe: skip_if_open
skip_if_unchanged:
  ref: __ORBIT_BASE_BRANCH__
  cursor:
    tags:
    - code-review
    - no-diff-expected
    - auto-task:code-review
    legacy_tags:
    - code-review-sweep
    - no-diff-expected

code-review.75692b4c526690c43e859bc66f5d336390ed1927:
schemaVersion: 1
name: code-review
description: Steady whole-tree code review that reviews the two least recently reviewed modules in full
enabled: false
schedule:
  cron: 40 */6 * * *
template:
  title: Review the two least recently reviewed modules
  description: |-
    Review this workspace's whole tree a little at a time: partition the tracked
    tree into modules, pick the two modules reviewed least recently, and read
    both in full at one pinned commit. The durable output is filed Orbit tasks
    for every confirmed finding plus the recorded rotation and cursor records;
    the execution summary is the audit trail. Narrative-only output does not
    count as delivery. This is not a review of a merged-commit window: a
    whole-module read also finds defects older than any recent change, and
    per-delivery diff review is a separate concern owned elsewhere.

    ## Rules and command surfaces

    - Use the registered Orbit tool surface. List prior rotation sweeps, newest
      first, with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["done"],"type":"chore","tag":["code-review","no-diff-expected","auto-task:code-review"],"limit":50,"fields":["id","created_at"],"model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      If the envelope reports `truncated`, repeat with a larger `limit` until it
      does not, so no completed sweep is left out of the rotation history.
      Both tag filters use AND semantics. The `auto-task:code-review`
      provenance tag is carried only by tasks minted from this definition, so a
      hand-filed or full-review chore that shares the other tags is never a
      rotation sweep, and a finding is a `bug` tagged only `code-review`, so it
      is never a sweep either.
      For each listed sweep, discover its artifacts before fetching any record:
      list them with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.show --input '{"id":"<id>","field":"artifacts","model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      and fetch the rotation record with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.artifact.get --input '{"id":"<id>","path":"reviewed-modules.json","model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      only when that listing names `reviewed-modules.json`.
      Search existing coverage with
      `orbit tool run orbit.search --input '{"query":"<distinctive symptom, symbol, or file terms>","kind":"task","all":true,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      and list open review work with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["backlog","in-progress","proposed","blocked"],"tag":"code-review","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      File a confirmed high or critical finding as its own task with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.add --input '{"title":"<title>","description":"<markdown>","acceptance_criteria":["<observable outcome>"],"complexity":"medium","tags":["code-review"],"context_files":["file:<evidence source path>","file:<matching test path>"],"priority":"<low|medium|high|critical>","type":"bug","relations":[{"type":"spawned_from","target":"<this task ID>"},{"type":"regression_from","target":"<culprit task ID>","regression":{"nature":"<nature>","escape":"<escape>"}}],"workspace":"<current workspace path>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      File a module's grouped medium and low findings as its single cleanup task with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.add --input '{"title":"<title>","description":"<markdown listing every grouped finding>","acceptance_criteria":["<observable outcome>"],"complexity":"medium","tags":["code-review"],"context_files":["file:<evidence source path>","file:<matching test path>"],"priority":"<low|medium>","type":"bug","relations":[{"type":"spawned_from","target":"<this task ID>"},{"type":"regression_from","target":"<culprit task ID>","regression":{"nature":"<nature>","escape":"<escape>"}}],"workspace":"<current workspace path>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      In the grouped payload, `context_files` is the deduplicated union of every
      grouped finding's selectors, and `relations` carries at most one
      classified `regression_from` entry per distinct culprit task among the
      attributable grouped findings (omit it for a finding no task can be held
      responsible for, and say why in the description; keep every grouped
      finding listed in the description, including findings that share a
      culprit; when grouped findings sharing a culprit have conflicting nature
      or escape classifications, note them in the description and classify the
      single `regression_from` link `unclassified`). In either payload, omit
      the `regression_from` relation only when no landed task can be held
      responsible. Derive canonical `file:` selectors from every evidenced
      source path, removing the line suffix, and add the matching
      regression-test location. Use existing paths where possible; for a test file
      that must be created, set `allow_missing_context: true` and identify that
      intended path. Never file a finding without context selectors.
      Do not use direct lifecycle CLI subcommands; they skip agent provenance.
    - Fail open. A run whose two modules hold no confirmed findings is a
      successful no-op. Do not invent work to justify the run.

    ## Pin the commit

    Fetch the workspace's integration branch and record the full 40-character
    SHA of its tip. Partition, selection counts and every read use the tree as
    it stands at that SHA (`git show <sha>:<path>` when the checkout has
    moved), so later merges cannot shift a module under the review.

    ## Partition the tree into modules

    The module bound is **25,000 tracked text lines**, a maximum, not a target
    that may be exceeded. This is the same partition rule the whole-tree
    snapshot review uses, with no language- or toolchain-specific rule, so both
    definitions agree on what a module is. Inventory tracked files with
    `git ls-tree -r -z <sha>` and count each text blob at that SHA
    (`git show <sha>:<path>`), including an unterminated final line. Do not
    measure the moving checkout or count a concatenated archive containing
    binary files. Include source, tests, documentation and authored assets,
    including files at the root. Vendored, generated, binary and
    lockfile-only content may be excluded; record every excluded path and its
    reason in the execution summary and in `reviewed-modules.json`.

    Start with directory boundaries: take directories as candidates first.
    Recursively split every candidate above 25,000 lines into disjoint child
    directories, keeping files directly in the parent as separate candidates.
    If a leaf directory is still too large, split it into disjoint file sets.
    Prefer module boundaries where they fit the bound; the bound takes
    precedence. Group small, closely related candidates only when their
    combined count stays within the bound. Every included file must belong to
    exactly one module. Use `dir:` selectors for whole directories and `file:`
    selectors for direct files or file sets; never select an entire parent
    alongside its children in different modules. A module's ID is its
    selectors: the module's selectors sorted lexicographically and joined with
    `,`. Before selecting, verify all module counts against the bound and
    reconcile the inventories for gaps and duplicates. If a single included
    file exceeds 25,000 lines and this rule cannot produce a bounded module
    covering it, report `review_incomplete` with that uncovered path and
    count; do not file an oversized module review, silently exclude the file,
    or record it as reviewed.

    ## Build the last-reviewed map and select two modules

    The last-reviewed map comes only from `reviewed-modules.json` artifacts on
    done chores carrying `auto-task:code-review`, read as above — never from
    execution-summary prose, `sweep-cursor.json`, or a finding. Work through
    the listed sweeps newest first (newer `created_at` first, the
    lexicographically smaller task ID winning an equal timestamp): the first
    record that names a module ID is that module's most recent review, giving
    its review time (that sweep's `created_at`) and its pinned SHA. A sweep
    whose artifact listing has no `reviewed-modules.json`, or whose record is
    unreadable, malformed or names another schema version, counts as
    reviewing nothing — legacy window sweeps reviewed nothing in this
    rotation. Ignore modules the current partition no longer contains.

    A module that grew past the bound since its last review is split by the
    partition above, and each child inherits the last-reviewed time and pinned
    SHA of the module it was split from: when a current module has no record
    under its own ID, expand each recorded module's selectors to the file set
    they covered at that record's pinned SHA, and a current module whose
    files are a subset of one recorded module's files inherits that record.
    When more than one recorded module covers a current module's files, it
    inherits the oldest of their last-reviewed times and that record's pinned
    SHA.

    Count the commits since the last review for every module: for a reviewed
    or inheriting module, the number of commits in
    `<last reviewed pinned SHA>..<pinned SHA>` that touch the module's paths
    (`git rev-list --count <from>..<pinned SHA> -- <module paths>`); for a
    never-reviewed module, every commit up to the pinned SHA that touches its
    paths. Order all current modules by: never-reviewed first; then oldest
    last-reviewed time; then more commits since the last review; then the
    smaller module ID. Select the first **2** (every module when the partition
    holds fewer than 2). Record the ordering evidence — each selected
    module's last-reviewed time and pinned SHA or never-reviewed state, its
    commit count, and its ID — in the execution summary.

    ## Review the two selected modules in full

    Read each selected module in full at the pinned SHA, not a diff. On the
    first read, divide its inventory into stable named read partitions of at
    most 10,000 lines each. Prefer directory and module boundaries; split
    files larger than a partition into explicit inclusive line ranges. Cover
    every included line exactly once, with no gaps or overlaps, and include
    empty files in the inventory. Read every partition in full. Use parallel
    read passes or subagents when the crew and execution rules support them;
    otherwise read partitions sequentially. The reviewer remains responsible
    for reconciling every partition and checking calls and invariants across
    their boundaries. A search, summary, sampled read or truncated tool
    response does not count as a full read; continue in chunks until all
    lines in the partition have been examined.

    Look for:
    - correctness: logic errors, wrong edge cases, broken invariants between
      callers and callees;
    - error handling: swallowed or mislabelled errors, panics reachable from
      input, partial writes left behind on failure;
    - concurrency: races, lock ordering, locks held across awaits, unbounded
      or leaked tasks;
    - security boundaries: path traversal, injection, trust of unvalidated
      input, secrets in logs or output;
    - resource bounds: unbounded buffers, queues, retries, recursion or file
      growth;
    - conformance to the repository's documented standards: its agent guide,
      contributing guide, standards documents and lint configuration;
    - tests that do not test what they claim: assertions that cannot fail,
      fixtures that bypass the code under test, names that promise behavior
      the body never exercises.

    If full reading of a selected module cannot be met, do not record that
    module as reviewed and do not claim a clean no-op for it: return
    `result.blocker` with `kind: review_incomplete` and evidence naming each
    uncovered partition, file or unread line range and unresolved check, and
    put the same inventory in the execution summary. Only a module with every
    partition fully read and checks across partitions resolved counts as
    reviewed in this run.

    ## Attribute each finding to the task that introduced it

    Name the task that caused each finding when a landed task can be held
    responsible. Find the commit that introduced the defect (`git log -L` or
    `git blame` on the offending lines at the pinned SHA) and read the task ID
    from that commit: squash-merge subjects carry it as `[<task-id>]`, and
    the delivery's pull request references it otherwise. Confirm with
    `orbit.task.show` that the task exists and that its change is the one at
    fault — blame the commit that introduced the defect, not a later commit
    that merely touched the same file. When the defect spans several tasks'
    changes, blame the one whose change made the code wrong. When the culprit
    commit carries no task ID, or the defect predates every task that can be
    held responsible and was only exposed later, say so in the finding and
    file it without the relation rather than blaming a bystander. A
    whole-module review reaches defects far older than any recent change;
    age alone never makes a bystander responsible.

    ## File confirmed findings

    Verify every finding against the code at the pinned SHA before filing — a
    line that looks wrong but is guarded elsewhere is not a finding. Search
    open Orbit tasks tagged `code-review` before filing; skip duplicates and
    nitpicks. Give each confirmed finding a severity — `critical`, `high`,
    `medium` or `low` — used as the filed task's priority, file:line evidence
    at the pinned SHA, the `code-review` tag, and its module's ID.

    File each confirmed `critical` or `high` finding as its own `bug` task.
    Group a module's `medium` and `low` findings into at most one cleanup
    `bug` per module: it lists each grouped finding with its title, severity,
    file:line evidence and culprit task or the reason none can be held
    responsible; its `context_files` are the deduplicated union of the
    grouped findings' selectors; its priority is the highest grouped severity
    (`medium` when any grouped finding is medium, otherwise `low`); and it
    carries at most one classified `regression_from` relation per distinct
    culprit task among the attributable grouped findings (when findings sharing
    a culprit differ in nature or escape, note both in the description and
    classify the single link `unclassified`). A module with no medium or low findings files no cleanup
    task. Never group a high or critical finding into a cleanup task, and
    never file more than one cleanup task for one module in one run.

    Classify every `regression_from` relation you file by adding
    `"regression":{"nature":"<nature>","escape":"<escape>"}` to it.
    Choose `unclassified` rather than guess. `nature` is what kind of regression
    the link records:
    - `broke_existing`: the culprit broke behavior that worked before it landed.
    - `defect_in_new`: the defect is in code the culprit itself introduced.
    - `incomplete`: the culprit shipped without part of what its task required.
    - `merge_reintroduced`: a merge restored code or assets an earlier change had removed.
    - `contract_drift`: docs, schemas or a contract drifted from the behavior the culprit shipped.
    - `unclassified`: the evidence does not settle the nature.
    `escape` is why the delivery gates missed it:
    - `no_test`: no test covered the broken behavior.
    - `test_not_selected`: a covering test existed but the delivery's gates did not run it.
    - `platform_only`: it shows only on a platform or host the gates did not exercise.
    - `review_missed`: it was visible in the diff and review did not flag it.
    - `spec_ambiguous`: the task or spec left the expected behavior open to the shipped reading.
    - `nondeterministic`: it depends on timing, ordering or environment and passed when gated.
    - `unclassified`: the evidence does not settle the escape.

    When a finding is a repair that narrows a shared invariant — what the host
    will create, what URLs are accepted, what counts as first-party, or any
    other predicate with more than one caller — search for every caller and
    fixture of that predicate and name them in the filed task's description;
    its acceptance criteria must require the same change to update all of
    them together, not just the call site that produced the observed symptom.

    A pull request that is green only against its own base is not evidence
    the merged tree is green. When the finding shares an invariant with other
    in-flight work, the filed task's acceptance criteria must require
    comparing the per-commit suite on the integration branch against its
    parent commit, not just a green check on the PR's own base.

    On every completed run, write the rotation record to
    `.orbit/tmp/reviewed-modules.json` and attach it with
    `orbit tool run orbit.task.artifact.put --input '{"id":"<this task ID>","source_path":".orbit/tmp/reviewed-modules.json","path":"reviewed-modules.json","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.

    `{"schema_version":1,"ref":"<integration branch>","pinned_sha":"<full 40-character commit SHA>","modules":[{"id":"<module ID>","selectors":["<selector>"],"line_count":123,"filed_finding_ids":["<filed task ID>"]}],"exclusions":[{"path":"<path>","reason":"<reason>"}]}`.
    List exactly the modules this run fully reviewed (both selected modules,
    or every module when fewer than 2 exist), each with its ID, its selectors,
    its measured line count and the IDs of every task filed for its findings

    once when one was filed. A module this run did not fully read is never
    listed. The next run's last-reviewed map is built only from these
    records, so a completed run without one leaves its modules
    never-reviewed.

    cursor artifact, which the scheduler reads to decide whether the next
    tick has anything to review: write
    `{"schema_version":1,"ref":"<integration branch>","cursor":"<full 40-character commit SHA>"}`
    to a gitignored scratch file inside the checkout (for example
    `.orbit/tmp/sweep-cursor.json`) and attach it with
    `orbit tool run orbit.task.artifact.put --input '{"id":"<this task ID>","source_path":".orbit/tmp/sweep-cursor.json","path":"sweep-cursor.json","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
    `orbit tool show <tool.name>` prints the tool's schema.
    Write it on every completed run, including a run with no confirmed
    findings: the commit it names is the pinned SHA this run examined, and a
    completed run without it leaves the next tick no cursor to compare the
    branch tip against.

    Record in the execution summary the integration branch and pinned SHA,
    the partition (every module's ID, selectors and line count, with every
    exclusion and its reason), the selection ordering evidence for the two
    reviewed modules, per-partition reading coverage for each, and every
    filed task ID (naming the cleanup task's module and grouped findings, and
    each individual task's finding). State explicitly when a reviewed module
    held no confirmed findings.

  - The tracked tree was partitioned at one pinned integration-branch SHA into disjoint modules of at most 25,000 tracked text lines each, directory boundaries first, with every exclusion named, and the 2 modules selected were the least recently reviewed (never-reviewed first, then oldest last-reviewed time, then more commits since the last review, then the smaller module ID), or every module when fewer than 2 exist.

description: Post-merge code review of changes merged since the last completed sweep

schedule:

    output does not count as delivery.

    - Use the registered Orbit tool surface. Find the newest current-name sweep with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["done"],"type":"chore","tag":["code-review","no-diff-expected","auto-task:code-review"],"limit":1,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      and the newest legacy-name sweep with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["done"],"type":"chore","tag":["code-review-sweep","no-diff-expected"],"limit":1,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Both tag filters use AND semantics. Compare the first result from each
      newest-first list by `created_at`, with the lexicographically smaller task ID
      winning an equal timestamp, and read the selected sweep's cursor with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.show --input '{"id":"<id>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      A finding is a `bug` tagged only `code-review`, so it is never a sweep
      candidate even when it completed after the selected sweep. The
      `auto-task:code-review` provenance tag is carried only by tasks minted from
      this definition, so a hand-filed or full-review chore that shares the
      other tags never displaces a real sweep's cursor.
      Search existing coverage with
      `orbit tool run orbit.search --input '{"query":"<distinctive symptom, symbol, or file terms>","kind":"task","all":true,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      and list open review work with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["backlog","in-progress","proposed","blocked"],"tag":"code-review","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      File a finding with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.add --input '{"title":"<title>","description":"<markdown>","acceptance_criteria":["<observable outcome>"],"complexity":"medium","tags":["code-review"],"priority":"<low|medium|high|critical>","type":"bug","relations":[{"type":"regression_from","target":"<culprit task ID>"}],"workspace":"<current workspace path>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Omit `relations` only when no task in the window can be held responsible.
      Do not use direct lifecycle CLI subcommands; they skip agent provenance.
    - Fail open. A window with no confirmed findings is a successful no-op. Do not
      invent work to justify the run.

    ## Determine the review window

    Run both completed-sweep queries above and select the newer result using the
    stated ordering. Read the last-reviewed commit recorded in that sweep's
    execution summary, then review the commits from that point to the current HEAD
    of the workspace's integration branch. Never use a `code-review`-only finding
    as a cursor, and never treat a selected sweep's missing cursor as a first run.
    If neither sweep query returns a result, record the current HEAD as the baseline
    and stop — only that case seeds the cursor.

    ## Review the window

    Read the diffs white-box: correctness, concurrency and error handling, and
    conformance to the repository's documented standards (agent guide, contributing
    guide, lint configuration). Review the window as a whole — interactions between
    separately merged changes are findings per-change review cannot see.

    ## Attribute each finding to the task that introduced it

    Every finding is a regression from a change that landed in the window, so
    name the task that caused it. Find the commit that introduced the defect
    (`git log -L` or `git blame` on the offending lines, restricted to the
    reviewed range) and read the task ID from that commit: squash-merge subjects
    carry it as `[<task-id>]`, and the delivery's pull request references it
    otherwise. Confirm with `orbit.task.show` that the task exists and that its
    change is the one at fault — blame the commit that introduced the defect, not
    a later commit that merely touched the same file. When the defect spans
    several tasks' changes, blame the one whose change made the code wrong.
    When the culprit commit carries no task ID, or the defect predates the
    window and was only exposed by it, say so in the finding and file it without
    the relation rather than blaming a bystander.

    wrong but is guarded elsewhere is not a finding. Search open Orbit tasks tagged
    `code-review` before filing; skip duplicates and nitpicks. File each confirmed
    finding as its own Orbit task with file:line evidence, a severity-appropriate
    priority, the `code-review` tag, and a `regression_from` relation targeting
    the task identified above. The finding's description names the culprit task
    and the commit that introduced the defect.

    ## Findings that narrow a shared invariant

    When a finding is a repair that narrows a shared invariant — what the host
    will create, what URLs are accepted, what counts as first-party, or any
    other predicate with more than one caller — search for every caller and
    fixture of that predicate and name them in the filed task's description;
    its acceptance criteria must require the same change to update all of
    them together, not just the call site that produced the observed symptom.

    the merged tree is green. When the finding shares an invariant with other
    in-flight work, the filed task's acceptance criteria must require
    comparing the per-commit suite on the integration branch against its
    parent commit, not just a green check on the PR's own base.

    ## Record the cursor

    Always record the reviewed range and the new last-reviewed commit in the
    persisted execution summary — the next sweep's window starts there. Record
    the same commit as this task's machine-readable cursor artifact, which the
    scheduler reads to decide whether the next tick has anything to review:
    write `{"schema_version":1,"ref":"<integration branch>","cursor":"<full 40-character commit SHA>"}`
    to a gitignored scratch file inside the checkout (for example
    `target/sweep-cursor.json`) and attach it with
    `orbit tool run orbit.task.artifact.put --input '{"id":"<this task ID>","source_path":"target/sweep-cursor.json","path":"sweep-cursor.json","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
    Write it on every completed sweep, including an empty window: the commit it
    names is the one this sweep examined through, and a completed sweep without
    it leaves the next tick no cursor to compare the branch tip against.

  - Every filed finding carries a `regression_from` relation targeting the task whose landed commit introduced the defect, or its description states why no task in the window can be held responsible.
  - The reviewed range and the new last-reviewed commit are recorded in the persisted execution summary.
  - The new last-reviewed commit is attached as this task's `sweep-cursor.json` artifact (`schema_version` 1, the integration branch, and the full commit SHA).
  - A window with no confirmed findings succeeds as a no-op.
  task_type: chore
  tags:
  - code-review
  - no-diff-expected
  priority: medium
  complexity: hard

  # for configs written before that crew existed.

schemaVersion: 1
name: code-review
description: Steady whole-tree code review that reviews the two least recently reviewed modules in full
enabled: false
schedule:
  cron: 40 */6 * * *
template:
  title: Review the two least recently reviewed modules
  description: |-
    Review this workspace's whole tree a little at a time: partition the tracked
    tree into modules, pick the two modules reviewed least recently, and read
    both in full at one pinned commit. The durable output is filed Orbit tasks
    for every confirmed finding plus the recorded rotation and cursor records;
    the execution summary is the audit trail. Narrative-only output does not
    count as delivery. This is not a review of a merged-commit window: a
    whole-module read also finds defects older than any recent change, and
    per-delivery diff review is a separate concern owned elsewhere.

    ## Rules and command surfaces

    - Use the registered Orbit tool surface. List prior rotation sweeps, newest
      first, with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["done"],"type":"chore","tag":["code-review","no-diff-expected","auto-task:code-review"],"limit":50,"fields":["id","created_at"],"model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      If the envelope reports `truncated`, repeat with a larger `limit` until it
      does not, so no completed sweep is left out of the rotation history.
      Both tag filters use AND semantics. The `auto-task:code-review`
      provenance tag is carried only by tasks minted from this definition, so a
      hand-filed or full-review chore that shares the other tags is never a
      rotation sweep, and a finding is a `bug` tagged only `code-review`, so it
      is never a sweep either.
      For each listed sweep, discover its artifacts before fetching any record:
      list them with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.show --input '{"id":"<id>","field":"artifacts","model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      and fetch the rotation record with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.artifact.get --input '{"id":"<id>","path":"reviewed-modules.json","model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      only when that listing names `reviewed-modules.json`.
      Search existing coverage with
      `orbit tool run orbit.search --input '{"query":"<distinctive symptom, symbol, or file terms>","kind":"task","all":true,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      and list open review work with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["backlog","in-progress","proposed","blocked"],"tag":"code-review","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      File a confirmed high or critical finding as its own task with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.add --input '{"title":"<title>","description":"<markdown>","acceptance_criteria":["<observable outcome>"],"complexity":"medium","tags":["code-review"],"context_files":["file:<evidence source path>","file:<matching test path>"],"priority":"<low|medium|high|critical>","type":"bug","relations":[{"type":"spawned_from","target":"<this task ID>"},{"type":"regression_from","target":"<culprit task ID>","regression":{"nature":"<nature>","escape":"<escape>"}}],"workspace":"<current workspace path>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      File a module's grouped medium and low findings as its single cleanup task with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.add --input '{"title":"<title>","description":"<markdown listing every grouped finding>","acceptance_criteria":["<observable outcome>"],"complexity":"medium","tags":["code-review"],"context_files":["file:<evidence source path>","file:<matching test path>"],"priority":"<low|medium>","type":"bug","relations":[{"type":"spawned_from","target":"<this task ID>"},{"type":"regression_from","target":"<culprit task ID>","regression":{"nature":"<nature>","escape":"<escape>"}}],"workspace":"<current workspace path>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      In the grouped payload, `context_files` is the deduplicated union of every
      grouped finding's selectors, and `relations` carries at most one
      classified `regression_from` entry per distinct culprit task among the
      attributable grouped findings (omit it for a finding no task can be held
      responsible for, and say why in the description; keep every grouped
      finding listed in the description, including findings that share a
      culprit; when grouped findings sharing a culprit have conflicting nature
      or escape classifications, state the differing classifications in the
      description and classify the single `regression_from` link
      `unclassified`). In either payload, omit
      the `regression_from` relation only when no landed task can be held
      responsible. Derive canonical `file:` selectors from every evidenced
      source path, removing the line suffix, and add the matching
      regression-test location. Use existing paths where possible; for a test file
      that must be created, set `allow_missing_context: true` and identify that
      intended path. Never file a finding without context selectors.
      Do not use direct lifecycle CLI subcommands; they skip agent provenance.
    - Fail open. A run whose two modules hold no confirmed findings is a
      successful no-op. Do not invent work to justify the run.

    ## Pin the commit

    Fetch the workspace's integration branch and record the full 40-character
    SHA of its tip. Partition, selection counts and every read use the tree as
    it stands at that SHA (`git show <sha>:<path>` when the checkout has
    moved), so later merges cannot shift a module under the review.

    ## Partition the tree into modules

    The module bound is **25,000 tracked text lines**, a maximum, not a target
    that may be exceeded. This is the same partition rule the whole-tree
    snapshot review uses, with no language- or toolchain-specific rule, so both
    definitions agree on what a module is. Inventory tracked files with
    `git ls-tree -r -z <sha>` and count each text blob at that SHA
    (`git show <sha>:<path>`), including an unterminated final line. Do not
    measure the moving checkout or count a concatenated archive containing
    binary files. Include source, tests, documentation and authored assets,
    including files at the root. Vendored, generated, binary and
    lockfile-only content may be excluded; record every excluded path and its
    reason in the execution summary and in `reviewed-modules.json`.

    Start with directory boundaries: take directories as candidates first.
    Recursively split every candidate above 25,000 lines into disjoint child
    directories, keeping files directly in the parent as separate candidates.
    If a leaf directory is still too large, split it into disjoint file sets.
    Prefer module boundaries where they fit the bound; the bound takes
    precedence. Group small, closely related candidates only when their
    combined count stays within the bound. Every included file must belong to
    exactly one module. Use `dir:` selectors for whole directories and `file:`
    selectors for direct files or file sets; never select an entire parent
    alongside its children in different modules. A module's ID is its
    selectors: the module's selectors sorted lexicographically and joined with
    `,`. Before selecting, verify all module counts against the bound and
    reconcile the inventories for gaps and duplicates. If a single included
    file exceeds 25,000 lines and this rule cannot produce a bounded module
    covering it, report `review_incomplete` with that uncovered path and
    count; do not file an oversized module review, silently exclude the file,
    or record it as reviewed.

    ## Build the last-reviewed map and select two modules

    The last-reviewed map comes only from `reviewed-modules.json` artifacts on
    done chores carrying `auto-task:code-review`, read as above — never from
    execution-summary prose, `sweep-cursor.json`, or a finding. Work through
    the listed sweeps newest first (newer `created_at` first, the
    lexicographically smaller task ID winning an equal timestamp): the first
    record that names a module ID is that module's most recent review, giving
    its review time (that sweep's `created_at`) and its pinned SHA. A sweep
    whose artifact listing has no `reviewed-modules.json`, or whose record is
    unreadable, malformed or names another schema version, counts as
    reviewing nothing — legacy window sweeps reviewed nothing in this
    rotation. Ignore modules the current partition no longer contains.

    A module that grew past the bound since its last review is split by the
    partition above, and each child inherits the last-reviewed time and pinned

    Write it on every completed run, including a run with no confirmed
    findings: the commit it names is the pinned SHA this run examined, and a
    completed run without it leaves the next tick no cursor to compare the
    branch tip against.

    the partition (every module's ID, selectors and line count, with every
    exclusion and its reason), the selection ordering evidence for the two
    reviewed modules, per-partition reading coverage for each, and every
    filed task ID (naming the cleanup task's module and grouped findings, and
    each individual task's finding). State explicitly when a reviewed module
    held no confirmed findings.
